title: A population-adaptive genetic algorithm for topology optimization of liquid-cooled heat sinks
abstract: Genetic algorithm (GA)-based topology optimization (TO) has emerged as a promising approach for addressing conjugate heat transfer problems. While the GATO method offers numerous advantages due to its explicit and gradient-free character, the high computational cost remains a major limitation. This study aims to enhance the efficiency and practical applicability of GATO in the design and structural optimization of liquid-cooled heat sinks under heterogeneously heating conditions in electronic device thermal management. First, a systematic parametric investigation examines the influence of GA parameters (elite number, mutation rate, crossover scheme, and population size) on TO outcomes, identifying population size as the most influential factor. Motivated by this finding, we propose a Population-Adaptive Genetic Algorithm (PAGA), which dynamically reduces the population size in response to the objective function values during TO convergence. This strategy substantially reduces computational cost by over 50% without compromising solution quality. The effectiveness, robustness, and versatility of the PAGA-based TO framework are further demonstrated through optimization studies under diverse boundary and operating conditions, including varied inlet–outlet layouts, heat source distributions, and liquid coolants with distinct thermophysical properties. In all examined cases, the optimized flow channel configurations are physically consistent and thermally efficient due to their ability to spatially match cooling capacity with demand. For all coolants tested, TO-derived heat sinks consistently outperform the conventional straight-channel design in mitigating temperature hotspots, confirming the effectiveness and broad applicability of the proposed method.

title: Design and optimization of piezo-thermoelectric hybrid power generation in a small-scale thermoacoustic engine prototype
abstract: This study aims to design, build, and optimize the performance of a small-scale thermoacoustic engine (TAE) prototype hybrid (piezoelectric/thermoelectric) power generation. Independent variables are predicted using the quadratic model, which are selected based on ANOVA analysis for best fit of experimental data. A Box-Behnken Design (BBD) is applied with 20 treatments. The independent variables considered for evaluation included run time (5–15 min), hot-side heat exchanger (HX) temperature (400–600 °C), resonator length (0.402–0.604 m), cold-side HX temperature (0–27 °C) and working gas (air, N 2 , CO₂). The results show that the hot-side HX temperature had a significant impact on the total output power ( P total ), whereas the cold-side HX temperature and resonator length had a relatively mild effect on P total . The working gas type and run time also do not have a significant impact on P total . The optimal conditions for a maximum P total of 65 mW were achieved using nitrogen (N 2 ) as the working gas, under a hot-side HX temperature of 585 °C, resonator length of 0.518 m, and cold-side HX temperature of 2.025 °C. The good fit between experimental and predicted values under optimal conditions confirms the accuracy of the model. Results demonstrate this TAE potential for industrial waste heat recovery application, despite long-term material stability at high temperatures need to be further investigated.

title: Thermodynamic assessment of 3D fractional dual-phase lag thermal transport in annular cooling architectures for 3D-stacked ICs
abstract: The extreme volumetric power densities of 3D-stacked integrated circuits (3D-ICs) complicate thermal management by triggering non-Fourier, sub-diffusive heat transfer. The present work creates a framework for 3D thermal transport assessment within the annular cooling geometry, by using a fractional dual-phase lag approach to describe the thermal relaxation and sub-microsecond regimes. A high-precision hybrid spectral collocation marching method (HSCMM), based on the global Gauss–Lobatto–Legendre (GLL) grid, is developed to solve the nonlinear coupled fractional order and phase-lag dissimilarity equation with velocity profile. The developed solver shows a spectral accuracy in the convergence of the manifold. The results demonstrate a 27.10% improvement in the Performance Evaluation Criterion (PEC) in the presence of the fractional domain relative to the classical case. This work further proves that maximizing raw heat transfer is not always tantamount to thermodynamic efficiency. Notably, the sub-diffusive transport designs achieve up to 65.20% reduction in peak temperatures compared to the classical cooling baselines. These results offer a transformative design protocol for mitigating catastrophic thermal runaway in next-generation CMOS and high-density logic-on-memory architectures.

title: Semi-analytic model for the description of an earth-air thermal syphon as a passive air conditioning system
abstract: Passive air-conditioning systems composed by earth-air heat exchangers (EAHE) and solar chimneys (SC) are interesting alternatives for the cooling of small and medium spaces in an eco-sustainable way that does not require electricity. The current work presents a semi-analytical model that can predict the general airflow characteristics along the system, such as temperature, moisture content, pressure and velocity. The model requires to describe the buoyancy effects along the solar chimney, together with the convective heat transfer of the pipe flow along the EAHE. Fluid mechanics are coupled with heat transfer in solids, yielding the ability to not only describe the bulk airflow properties, but also the temperature field of the ground surrounding the EAHE. In order to solve this complex system of non linear partial differential equations several techniques are used, which include scale analysis, perturbation methods and Fourier expansions. The model is validated by means of analytical, numerical and experimental data from the literature that compares with the subsystems of the EAHE and SC separately and coupled. Finally, a simple parametrical analysis is performed for some geometrical aspects which includes the ratio between pipe lengths and radii, the ambient moisture content and the amount of solar chimneys. It is shown how the model performs a satisfactory description of the airflow behavior, rendering it as a promising first approximation tool that can help to choose between different geometrical configurations before committing with a large numerical fluid simulation or the construction of an experimental prototype for fine tuning of the system.

title: Mass transfer in porous media driven by electrophoretic motion of confined nanobubbles
abstract: In this work, a theoretical framework is developed for a new mass transfer mechanism in porous media driven by the electrophoretic motion of confined nanobubbles. Although nanobubbles have been investigated in a wide range of physicochemical contexts, their role as active fluid transport agents in porous structures has not, to our knowledge, been previously explored. The analysis couples confined Stokes flow around a translating nanobubble, electrophoretic mobility, porous-medium structural effects, and nanobubble size polydispersity. This formulation leads to a Darcy-type transport law relating the macroscopic volumetric flux to the applied electric field. In addition, explicit expressions are obtained for the optimal pore size that maximizes transport. A key result is the existence of an optimal confinement ratio, defined as the ratio between nanobubble diameter and pore diameter ¿, with a maximum at ¿* = 0.555, at which pumping power is maximized. At this optimum, the transport efficiency — defined as the fraction of displaced liquid contributing to net flow — is approximately 20%, reflecting the balance between hydrodynamic confinement and electrophoretic mobility. For polydisperse nanobubble populations, the optimal ratio shifts only weakly and the transport is affected only at second order in the dispersion, indicating that the mechanism is robust to realistic levels of size variability. Using representative physical parameters, the model predicts volumetric fluxes of up to 45 Lh^-1m^-2 under experimentally attainable electric fields. These results identify a previously unexplored electrohydrodynamic transport mechanism in porous media, in which electrophoretically driven nanobubbles act as microscopic displacement agents capable of converting electric forcing into macroscopic fluid motion

title: Impact of the Lee model coefficient on 3D CFD simulations of microgravity annular flow condensation with two-phase inlet conditions
abstract: This study investigates the sensitivity of three-dimensional Volume of Fluid (VOF) simulations of microgravity annular FC-72 condensation to the Lee phase-change relaxation coefficient. The computations reproduce parabolic-flight experiments for condensation in a circular tube of 7.12 mm inner diameter and 791.72 mm cooled length, using two-phase inlet conditions and experimentally derived axial wall heat-flux boundary conditions. Three microgravity operating cases are considered, spanning FC-72 mass fluxes of 129.0, 177.8, and 282.0 kg m −2 s −1 with inlet qualities of 0.89, 0.89, and 0.65, respectively. The Lee coefficient is varied over r i = 1 0 3 , 1 0 4 , and 5 × 1 0 4 s − 1 in order to examine its effect on interfacial thermal equilibrium, phase distribution, wall temperature, and local heat transfer coefficient. The results show that low r i leads to insufficient interfacial relaxation, broader thermal nonequilibrium, and underprediction of condensation heat transfer, whereas excessively large r i drives the interface strongly toward saturation but overpredicts the heat transfer level. Among the values tested, r i = 1 0 4 s − 1 provides the best agreement with experiment in terms of the condensation-section averaged heat transfer coefficient, with deviations of approximately 2%, 4%, and 1% for Cases 1–3, respectively. This agreement is for section-averaged quantities, while the local axial profiles still exhibit noticeable discrepancies in wall temperature and heat transfer coefficient trends. Using this selected coefficient, the fully three-dimensional simulations are also compared with two-dimensional axisymmetric results. The 3D framework substantially improves agreement with experiments and removes key deficiencies of the axisymmetric approximation, including artificial liquid accumulation near the tube centerline and unrealistically low wall-temperature predictions. The results demonstrate that accurate prediction of microgravity annular condensation in circular tubes with two-phase inlet conditions requires not only an appropriate phase-change relaxation coefficient, but also a three-dimensional representation of interfacial distribution. The framework developed here provides an improved basis for predicting averaged condensation heat-transfer behavior in two-phase space thermal management systems, while the remaining local discrepancies highlight the need for further refinement of the axial distribution of wall temperature and local heat transfer.

title: CFD-informed deep learning for gas concentration field reconstruction and hazard mapping in longwall goaf
abstract: Accurate and rapid prediction of gas concentration fields and hazard-zone evolution in longwall goaf environments is critical not only for preventing methane-related explosions and oxidation-driven spontaneous combustion, but also for efficient drainage management and methane abatement. However, conventional tools such as computational fluid dynamics (CFD), while capable of delivering accurate spatial distributions of goaf gas concentration, require substantial computation time, specialised commercial software, and expert knowledge for model setup and interpretation. These constraints limit their practicality for routine hazard assessment or responsive operational planning. To address this gap, this study presents an integrated framework in the domain of longwall goaf hazard assessment to couple high-fidelity CFD simulations with a multi-output deep neural network for near-instantaneous, CFD-equivalent predictions. A scalar-to-spatial multilayer perceptron (MLP) encoder transforms a single gas emission rate into a latent spatial representation, which is decoded by five task-specific U-Nets to produce oxygen and methane concentrations, oxidation and explosive zones, and synergistic hazard maps. Trained on 2000 CFD-generated scenarios covering 10–20,000 l/s emission rates, the model achieves PSNR > 40 dB, SSIM > 0.99, and R² > 0.99, while reducing computation time from ∼6 h to < 1 s. Sensitivity analysis shows that beyond an emission sampling interval of 20, SSIM drops sharply at interval 40, with CH₄ and synergistic hazard predictions more sensitive to sparsity than O₂ and oxidation outputs. Compared with a continuous conditional generative adversarial network (CcGAN), the hybrid model demonstrates superior structural coherence, stable and consistent responses to changes in emission rates, and strict boundary adherence, whereas CcGAN exhibits boundary distortions, excessive smoothing, and irregular local reversals. These advantages, together with its computational efficiency, position the hybrid model as a practical tool for generating high-resolution gas concentration and hazard maps on demand, enabling timely risk evaluation and proactive mitigation in underground longwall mining. It could also support more energy-efficient methane drainage and utilisation by guiding the targeted localisation of favourable drawdown zones and informing data-driven methane management strategies.

title: Application of a dual manifold topology-optimized pin fin cold plate for high heat flux thermal management of automotive power inverters
abstract: This study puts forward a new dual manifold topology-optimized pin fin cold plate to address the high heat flux thermal management of power conversion units in electric and hybrid vehicles. The optimized pin fin cold plate was experimentally investigated using six thick-film heaters, enabling heat fluxes up to 200 W/cm², with deionized water as the coolant, while temperature measurement and monitoring were performed using six high-accuracy Class A PT100 resistance temperature detectors. The numerical simulations were carried out for circular, elliptical, airfoiled (0-degree attack angle), and funnel pin fin shapes to enable systematic performance comparison. With a peak heat transfer coefficient of 18 kW/m²·℃, the optimized pin fin outperformed its counterparts, delivering a 47–66% enhancement in heat transfer, up to 19% lower thermal resistance relative to baseline fins, and a 15% reduction in pressure drop. Its thermal resistance ranges from 0.0249 to 0.0271 ℃/W, and pressure drop remains between 3 and 6.5 kPa. Topology‑optimized pin fins keep temperatures within the safe range, achieving 3.95% temperature uniformity, which is 54% better than the baseline. Compared to the baseline pin fin, the proposed new pin fin decreases the average module temperature by 12–14.5℃ and halves the end-to-end temperature variation. The improvements are mainly attributed to enhanced flow distribution and intensified boundary-layer disruption achieved by the spatially differentiated pin fin structure. Overall, the proposed topology-optimized cold plate exhibits nearly double the energy efficiency of the baseline pin fin design, as confirmed by figure of merit and performance evaluation criterion analyses, demonstrating its strong potential for advanced thermal management of high-power automotive electronics.

title: Fuzzy modelling and physics-informed neural networks for transpiration cooling with coolant phase change
abstract: This paper employs fuzzy modelling for transpiration cooling with coolant phase change in porous media. It discards the inaccurate empirical descriptions of fluid-solid heat transfer to ensure model accuracy and achieves solutions by a Physics-informed Neural Network (PINN) method. Typically, the lack of mathematical descriptions in fluid-solid heat transfer degrades the prediction accuracy of practical local thermal non-equilibrium (LTNE) effects in porous structures, thereby requiring data compensation in PINN strategies. To enhance the effectiveness of data compensation, this study explores three feature enhancement strategies, i.e., considering three additional losses concerned with the phase-change position, the positive fluid-solid temperature difference, and the fluid-solid temperature difference gradient along the flow direction, respectively. It is demonstrated that they effectively enhance the predictive accuracy of the two-phase region location, eliminate the non-physical sign inverse in fluid-solid temperature difference, and avoid non-physical spatial temperature gradients in the single-phase area. Using the three feature enhancement strategies, this study further evaluates the prediction results of the PINN strategy under various operating parameters. The PINN results are found to adhere to the same physical evolutionary behavior as the traditional numerical results, and their maximum temperature deviation is below 2.4%, confirming the PINN strategy’s high reliability. This study provides a novel simulation approach for the engineering systems of phase-change transpiration cooling without a precise and complete model.

title: Flow boiling heat transfer correlations in horizontal circular tubes: A review
abstract: Two-phase flow boiling is fundamental in the design of heat exchangers across diverse applications, from refrigeration to power generation systems. With the continuous growth of advanced power generation technologies, such as organic Rankine cycles (ORCs), this review systematically evaluates established correlation model approaches, assessing their physical foundations and predictive capabilities against experimental data representative of these applications. By analyzing each correlation type and examining its ability to capture the influence of key operating parameters (heat flux, mass velocity, and saturation temperature), this work demonstrates how the underlying assumptions of these models are rooted in the heat transfer mechanisms typical of refrigeration, characterized by low heat fluxes and low saturation temperatures, contrasting with the demanding operating conditions of power generation applications. Furthermore, this review compiles experimental results of the flow boiling heat transfer coefficient for low-GWP organic fluids in conventional tubes where existing correlations achieve acceptable accuracy ( MRAD < 20%) and presents them in an unconventional column-chart format that explicitly displays the operating and dimensionless parameter intervals characterizing each dataset. This visualization enables designers to identify which correlations are suitable for their specific operating conditions. The analysis reveals a critical finding: validated experimental datasets for all studied fluids cluster exclusively within the refrigeration-scale parameter space, with minimal representation of the high-heat flux, elevated-saturation temperature conditions typical of ORC systems. Consequently, for R1234yf , R1234ze(E) , R600a , and other low-GWP power-generation fluids, no ORC-relevant conditions for which there are validated correlations currently exist.

title: A monolithic enthalpy-based model for the simulation of in-flight ice accretion on heated bodies using moving finite elements
abstract: With aircraft icing occuring in more and more complex environments, its modelling and simulation remains a challenging task. This is particularly the case for ice crystal icing on a heated substrate where effects such as liquid-solid phase change and imbibition can take place. In this work an unsteady model for ice accretion and melting on a heated substrate is presented. The model is based on an enthalpy formulation that accounts for temperature and liquid volume fraction gradients inside the accretion layer. It also takes into account heat conduction inside the considered substrate. The model is formulated in terms of a partial differential equation expressed on the time-evolving domain, that is solved using a moving finite element method. After describing the model and numerical resolution scheme, a verification case based on the Stefan problem is performed. The method is then used to simulate a heated flat plate configuration in ice crystal icing conditions, for which experimental data is available. The simulations are first performed in one dimension and several properties of the methodology are assessed. In particular, the effect of taking the imbibition process into account is investigated. The capabilities of the proposed methodology are then demonstrated with a two dimensional simulation of the heated plate. The results show that the methodology is an interesting way forward for the numerical investigation of icing on heated bodies.

title: Hierarchical thermal design for battery packs using phase change materials
abstract: Effective thermal management remains a critical challenge in the design of lithium-ion battery packs, where non-uniform heating can degrade safety, performance, and operational lifetime. This study proposes a hierarchical, physics-informed optimization framework for battery pack cooling, integrating generative constructal design with multi-scale conjugate heat transfer simulations. The workflow addresses thermal management at three distinct levels. At the cell scale, phase change material is used to assist cooling, in combination with optimized high-conductivity annular fin structures, designed using a generative latent space approach. This reduces the number of design variables by over 95% compared to conventional pixel-wise topology optimization, while also enhancing the geometric diversity of the structures. At the module level, spatial variations in cell heating and boundary conditions are addressed by interpolating the latent space of optimized fin geometries across the cylindrical cell assembly. Functionally graded fin distributions adapt locally to thermal loads, reducing hotspot temperatures by up to 28.5% without increasing the total weight of the battery pack. This ensures improved thermal uniformity and aligns with constructal theory predictions. At the pack level, a bi-disperse porous media model is employed to optimize the cell packing density within each module, balancing hotspot temperature and pumping losses. We show that graded permeability fields can reduce hotspot temperatures by 60% compared to the lowest pumping power design, while only using 20% of the pumping power required by a uniform pack layout. The proposed generative constructal framework achieves substantial improvements in both thermal performance and computational efficiency, offering a scalable strategy for the design of safer, more energy-efficient, and longer-lasting battery systems.

title: Experimental study of downward flame spread over a thin cellulose-based sample in reduced and enhanced pressure
abstract: Downward flame spread, a canonical burning configuration, provides an effective platform for investigating material flammability and fire dynamics owing to its steady characteristics. Previous studies primarily employed reduced-pressure environments to simulate flame behavior in micro- and partial-gravity using pressure-modelling approaches. Although reduced-pressure effects have been extensively examined and several correlations relating flame spread behavior to ambient pressure have been proposed, their validity under elevated pressures remains largely unexplored. This experimental study investigates flame spread behavior over a thin filter paper under both reduced and enhanced pressures relative to atmospheric conditions and examines extinction phenomena at low pressure. Experiments were conducted in a combustion chamber over a wide pressure range (30–250 kPa). At high pressures, the flame exhibits a flat front across the sample width and spreads steadily downward. As pressure decreases from 250 to 60 kPa, flame height remains approximately constant while the sample heating length increases, attributed to enhanced thermal diffusion at reduced pressure. The flame spread rate was also determined. At high pressures, the measured spread rate agrees with the predicted thermal-regime value ( V f , th ) , whereas at lower pressures it decreases approximately linearly with inverse pressure, following V f / V f , th ≈ 1 − C / P . Below 50 kPa, the flame becomes dimmer and develops a curved front, and partial flame spread is observed. Periodic local extinction and regrowth along the flame width produce oscillations and lateral swinging until complete extinction occurs. Analysis indicates that reduced flame spread rates and extinction at low pressure result from increased radiative losses and diminished chemical kinetics.

title: A technical assessment of thermoelectric generator integration for waste heat recovery in air preheaters and effluent reactor pipelines of the carbon black industry
abstract: Carbon black production is widely recognised as an energy-intensive industrial activity with a substantial environmental footprint. A major challenge in its manufacture lies in the significant thermal energy losses associated with continuous high-temperature processes, spanning both high and medium temperature ranges, which reduce overall energy efficiency while increasing gaseous emissions. This study evaluates the feasibility of reducing these losses through the integration of thermoelectric generators (TEGs) for waste heat recovery in two representative units of the carbon black production process. The first is an air-to-air heat exchanger (APH) in the pelletizing section, operating at temperatures around 500 °C. The second is a reactor effluent duct located downstream of the reactor, where the process gas must be cooled to meet downstream operational and safety requirements, with temperatures decreasing from 700 °C to 300 °C. The analysis is based on real operating data and employs commercially available Bi₂Te₃-based thermoelectric modules operated within their allowable temperature limits. A one-dimensional thermo-resistive model is developed to describe heat transfer across the process gas, refractory lining, thermoelectric modules, and cooling system. A systematic sensitivity and optimization analysis is performed to assess the influence of refractory properties, thickness, and cooling strategies—including natural convection and forced convection with air and water—under realistic industrial constraints. All proposed cooling configurations rely exclusively on existing plant utilities and require minimal modifications to the current infrastructure. It is demonstrated that electrical power can be generated using TEGs with appropriate thermal configurations. The main limitation is gas-side convection, making thermal design crucial. Overall, the carbon black process is shown to be a viable environment for TEG application under medium- and high-temperature industrial conditions.

title: Boiling enhancement through acoustically assisted bubble departure
abstract: Boiling has been extensively studied over the past several decades due to its critical role in thermal-fluidic systems for power generation and electronics thermal management. By exploiting the large latent heat, boiling offers exceptional heat dissipation rate and remarkable wall temperature uniformity for power-dense applications. Typically, boiling performance is characterized by two key parameters. The first one is the critical heat flux (CHF), which is the maximum heating power per unit area (aka heat flux) that can be removed from the heat transfer surface before burnout. The second parameter is the heat transfer coefficient (HTC), which is the measure of cooling efficiency often described by the heat flux per unit superheat (excess wall temperature above saturation). Conventional boiling enhancement strategies rely primarily on surface modifications that employ micro/nanostructuring and/or chemical functionalization, which are neither durable nor well suited to handling transient heating loads. In this work, we introduce robust ultrasonic acoustic waves as an externally imposed and dynamically tunable approach to actively manipulate bubble nucleation, growth, and departure during nucleate boiling for heat transfer gain. Experiments were conducted on smooth copper plates (heated area = 15 mm × 15 mm) using degassed pure ethanol (200 proof, purity > 99.9%). By systematically varying the acoustic pressure amplitude ( P inc = 0–460 kPa) and wave incidence angle ( α = 0°–90°), we identified an optimal forcing condition. The heat dissipation rate is maximum when P inc = 46 kPa at α = 45°, consistent with our COMSOL simulation. Under optimal forcing, the CHF increased from ≈ 45 W/cm 2 to ≈ 72 W/cm 2 . We attribute the ≈ 60% enhancement in CHF to expedited bubble departure as observed by ≈ 36% reduction in departure diameter and ≈ 100% increase in departure frequency. A physics-based framework that is grounded on the dimensionless Bond number, which compares buoyancy and capillary forces, and the acoustic-capillary pressure ratio, which quantifies acoustic forcing relative to interfacial stability, shows that moderate forcing enhances bubble growth and departure while excessive forcing initiates interfacial destabilization that leads to bubble coalescence. The experiments further reveal a non-monotonic effect of forcing amplitude on boiling wherein weak forcing provides limited benefits whereas excessive forcing impacts CHF unfavorably. Collectively, these results establish boiling enhancement through acoustically assisted bubble departure as a robust and tunable strategy for on-demand transient thermal management of power-dense electronic devices.

title: Predicted effects of rectangular geometry on a hydrogen-based direct reduced iron shaft furnace
abstract: The use of pure hydrogen (H 2 ) as the reducing agent, instead of carbon monoxide (CO) containing syngas, in direct reduced iron (DRI) processes is limited by heat management in DRI shaft furnaces (SFs) due to hydrogen’s low volumetric density and the strongly endothermic reduction reactions. In conventional SFs with radial injections, the large lateral distance between the injection wall and the furnace centre results in a progressive imbalance between convective H 2 supply and consumption by endothermic reactions as the injected gas travels inward, leading to both lower H 2 concentrations and temperatures toward the furnace centre, which consequently causes incomplete reduction of the iron ore and compromised DRI quality. To overcome these limitations, we numerically explored a rectangular furnace (RF) geometry, which reduces the maximum lateral distance between the sidewalls where the hot reducing gas is injected and the furnace centre, thereby shortening the path over which H 2 is depleted and inlet sensible enthalpy is consumed. A steady-state multiphase Eulerian computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model of the reaction zone, integrated with the unreacted shrinking core model (USCM) and validated against published MIDREX SF data under syngas operation, was developed to simulate gas-solid reactive flows in (a) a conventional cylindrical SF and (b) rectangular furnaces with cross-sections of different length-to-width ratios. Our simulations predict that the RF geometry could potentially enhance the minimum metallization rate ( MR min ) of the DRI from 54.4% in the cylindrical SF to 98.2% in the RF and slightly improve the gas utilization rate ( UR ) from 24.3% to 25.5% (example results for 1.5 times the baseline hot gas flow rate of around 74 Nm 3 /s). These numerical findings suggest there are opportunities for innovative shaft furnace geometry designs to optimise H 2 -based DRI process, which is until now an under explored design factor. We acknowledge there are practical challenges to fabricate and operate rectangular shaft furnaces that must be addressed before experimental validation and pilot scale testing to confirm the RF performances predicted by our simulations.

title: Two-phase measurement of flow boiling in a vertical narrow annular channel
abstract: The study of boiling flow is crucial for designing safety features of chemical and nuclear plants. The boiling behavior and bubble dynamics depend on various system parameters such as pressure, subcooling, mass flux, heat flux, and flow geometry. While flow boiling has been widely investigated, comprehensive experimental datasets covering a broad range of operating conditions remain limited. A new dataset of upward flow boiling is therefore collected using an annular test section with a heated inner rod. The test section has an inner diameter of 25.4 mm and an outer diameter of 38.10 mm, with a heated inner rod of 3 m length. Newly developed five-sensor conductivity probes by the authors are adopted to measure void fraction, gas velocity, and interfacial area concentration following a two-group description. Their dedicated sensor pattern allows the probes to traverse across the narrow channel with minimized near-wall blind zones. In addition, high-speed visualization is conducted recording axial flow evolution, based on which the Onset of Nucleate Boiling (ONB) and Point of Net Vapor Generation (PNVG) are identified. Parametric studies are also presented investigating the flow field dependence on systematic boundary conditions. This work presents valuable experimental data on flow boiling and two-phase flow measurements.

title: Pool boiling heat transfer on silicon surfaces with re-entrant microcavities and micropillars
abstract: High heat flux removal in advanced thermal management systems often relies on pool boiling, where surface microstructures strongly influence bubble dynamics and heat transfer. The geometry of these microstructures determines the critical heat flux (CHF) and the heat transfer coefficient (HTC). In this study, we experimentally investigate pool boiling of de-ionized water on silicon surfaces with re-entrant and vertical microcavities, re-entrant and vertical micropillars, and flat silicon surfaces. The CHF of re-entrant cavities is ≈ 142 W/cm 2 , representing ≈ 97% enhancement over vertical cavities (≈72 W/cm 2 ) and ≈ 43% over flat polished surfaces (≈99 W/cm 2 ). This improvement in CHF is attributed to the overhang geometry or hoodoo, which lowers the temperature locally at the cavity rim to sustain liquid replenishment, and accelerates bubble departure through the necked cross-section. In contrast, re-entrant pillars did not improve CHF, reaching ≈ 133 W/cm 2 versus ≈ 140 W/cm 2 for vertical pillars, as vapor trapping in re-entrant pillars promotes bubble coalescence and early transition to film boiling. Comparison of HTC values indicate that re-entrant features offer marginal benefits for cavities. However, HTC increased for micropillars because of enhanced bubble ebullition cycle. Furthermore, increasing the cap thickness from 0.5 µm to 2 µm enhanced the CHF of re-entrant microcavity surfaces from ≈ 136 W/cm 2 to ≈ 156 W/cm 2 . In contrast, the CHF of re-entrant micropillar surfaces remained unaffected when the cap thickness increased from 0.5 µm to 2 µm. Furthermore, our heat transfer measurements show that for both re-entrant cavity and re-entrant pillars, the wall superheat at the onset of nucleate boiling (ONB) decreased by ≈ 3-4 K, a result that points to the overall impact of re-entrant geometry on boiling. By elucidating the heat transfer mechanism, the new findings reported in this study provide useful insights that can guide the design of engineered surfaces for cooling next-generation power-dense electronics.

title: Synergistic effect of thermal barrier coating and internal oil cooling for high-temperature turbine blades
abstract: With the continuous increase in turbine inlet temperature, turbine blades are exposed to extremely high thermal loads, for which single cooling or insulation strategies are no longer sufficient. In this study, a conjugate heat transfer model incorporating a multilayer wall structure consisting of a thermal barrier coating, bond coat, substrate, and an internally fuel-cooled channel is developed and validated against experimental temperature measurements for both uncoated and coated blades. On this basis, the coupled effects of coating thickness, external thermal load, and internal cooling capacity on blade thermal response are systematically investigated. The results indicate that increasing the coating thickness from 0 to 0.2 mm reduces the maximum wall temperature by approximately 85–129 K and decreases the temperature non-uniformity by about 26%–29% under external gas temperatures of 1200–1500 K. Further thickening to 0.5 mm, however, yields less than 20 K of additional temperature reduction, suggesting a pronounced diminishing-return effect. As the external gas temperature increases, the peak-temperature-based cooling effectiveness increment Δηmax rises from about 10.9% to 12.0%, demonstrating that the insulation advantage of the coating becomes more prominent under higher thermal loads. In contrast, increasing the coolant inlet temperature weakens this benefit, while enhancing the coolant mass flow rate significantly amplifies the coating-induced temperature reduction. These findings indicate that an optimal coating thickness of approximately 0.2 mm achieves a favorable balance between peak temperature suppression and temperature uniformity, and that the coating performance is governed by the coupled interaction between external heat load and internal heat transfer capability.

title: Simulations of heat transfer in corrugated channels using LES and RANS with algebraic flux models
abstract: Corrugated plate heat exchangers are widely used in industry, so obtaining reliable predictions of their thermal efficiency through numerical simulation is a major challenge. Due to limited computational resources, Reynolds averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) methods are widely used for this purpose, but they have shortcomings when it comes to studying high-Reynolds-number flows in this type of complex geometry. The objectives of this study are : (i) to propose an analysis of heat transfer via Large Eddies Simulations (LES), and to propose a predictive model for heat flux at the wall. (ii) To establish the limitations of the models used by the RANS method, in this case three common algebraic flux models (AFM), for the resolution of heat transfer. (iii) To propose a method for improving the prediction of these models with regard to heat flux at the wall. Using finely resolved large eddy simulations along with the periodic resolution method for the temperature transport equation, the structure of the temperature and of the wall heat flux are analyzed for various corrugation patterns, with corrugation angles β ranging from 15° to 45° and for a range of Reynolds numbers from Re = 4,721 to 47,025. The importance of the contact points between the upper and lower walls, characteristic of our geometrical setting, is highlighted for the intensification of the heat flux, pressure drop, and turbulence generation. The generalized Lévêque equation is shown to provide a very good estimate of the mean wall heat flux over the full range of Reynolds numbers and geometries, once the head loss coefficient is known accurately, confirming the close connection between head loss and heat transfer mechanisms. The LES results are further used to assess the performances of the modeling of the heat flux with RANS approach. Predictions of three commonly used AFM are compared, namely those based on the Simple Gradient Diffusion Hypothesis (SGDH), the Generalized Gradient Diffusion Hypothesis (GGDH) and the Higher Order Gradient Diffusion Hypothesis (HGDH). For such complex geometries, the predictions of the various AFM with standard parameter values deviate significantly from the reference results, with errors of the order of 100% for the maximum Reynolds number reached in this study. The accuracy of Nusselt number predictions obtained using the RANS method can be significantly improved by adjusting the model parameters, resulting in an average error of less than 20% across the entire range of Re for each β . However, once optimized, it is shown that all those AFM give exactly the same prediction for the wall heat flux. Nevertheless, even if good predictions of the heat transfer coefficient can be achieved, significant discrepancies remain in the RANS prediction of the turbulent heat flux.

title: Coupled dynamics of ripple waves and wetting-front boiling
abstract: Thin liquid films sheared by high-speed gas flows are widely used for cooling and heat transfer systems, yet the interaction between interfacial waves and nucleate boiling near dryout remains unclear. In this study, we examine the coupled dynamics of ripple waves and wetting-front boiling in a water film subjected to a fast air stream flowing over a heated wall using synchronized high-speed visualization up to 100 kHz, infrared thermography, and laser-induced fluorescence measurements. Under a liquid film Weber number below unity, the film exhibits ripple waves without disturbance waves. Wall heating stabilizes the shear instability by thickening the gaseous vorticity layer, resulting in longer wavelengths that are quantitatively reproduced by Kelvin–Helmholtz and Rayleigh–Taylor instability models extended to non-isothermal conditions. Near the wetting front, nucleate boiling initiates preferentially at ripple wave troughs, where bubbles grow rate-controlled by thermal diffusion within the thin film under the present experimental condition. Bubble bursting generates dry-patches that expand approximately linearly in time before being rewetted by incoming ripple wave crest. Furthermore, bubble growth beneath a ripple wave crest lifts the crest and enhances aerodynamic fragmentation, producing spreading droplets through a pathway distinct from conventional boiling entrainment and disturbance wave entrainment. These comprehensive results reveal how ripple wave instability and aerodynamic forces jointly couple nucleate boiling and droplet generation near the wetting front.

title: Development of a subgrid-scale liquid film condensation model for use in Euler-Euler computational multiphase flow simulations
abstract: Accurate numerical modelling of liquid film condensation is essential due to its significant influence in numerous industrial applications. The very small scale of this heat and mass transfer phenomenon motivates the development of a subgrid-scale film condensation model in this study. The developed model, for use in the computational multi-fluid dynamics Euler-Euler approach, provides physical closure for interfacial transfers when the film thickness is smaller than the near-wall mesh resolution. For pure vapour conditions, the rate of condensation is determined from the local liquid film thickness by considering pure conduction across a laminar film. The model aims to be applicable to internal convective condensation with significant shear stress at the gas-liquid interface. Moreover, the model is intended to cover all range of non-condensable gas concentration by considering both the thermal resistance of the liquid film and thermal resistance due to non-condensable gases and iteratively predicting the saturation temperature at the gas-liquid interface. A validation of the proposed model has been carried out through comparisons with an analytical model and experimental data from literature. The model has been evaluated under a wide range of operating conditions, including both pure vapour conditions and vapour mixtures with non-condensable gases. The developed model offers a satisfactory prediction of the energy transfer and condensate dynamics for laminar liquid film condensation in vertical tubes.

title: A closed-form homothetic model for the convective sublimation of dry ice
abstract: Dry ice sublimation governs mass loss, storage duration, and transport performance in carbon management and temperature-controlled applications. Existing predictive approaches are often computationally intensive or restricted to specific geometries and operating conditions of the system. In this study, we developed a closed-form analytical model for the time-dependent sublimation of solid CO2 under natural and forced convection. The formulation combines the interfacial energy balance, convective heat transfer scaling, and homothetic geometric retraction, yielding an explicit expression for the remaining solid mass in terms of the fluid properties, thermal driving potential, geometry, and initial conditions. The model is parameterized by the coefficient K_s and exponent γ, which are obtained from convection correlations and geometric scaling. Validation against independent experimental data from the literature showed good agreement for cylindrical pellets in low-velocity flow and dry-ice blocks under natural convection. Because maximizing the sublimation time is relevant to storage and transport, the design-oriented application of the model focused on natural convection. Under the examined conditions, the geometry that maximizes the sublimation time is governed by the competition between compactness and convective response, rather than by compactness alone. Therefore, the proposed model provides a simple and physically transparent framework for predicting dry-ice sublimation and comparing storage geometries.

title: On the complex interplay of temperature, phase change and natural convection in self-pressurization—an investigation using segregated modeling
abstract: Accurate prediction of self-pressurization in cryogenic tanks requires resolving the coupled effects of heat ingress, natural convection, and phase change. This work introduces a segregated numerical framework in which the liquid and vapor phases are treated with incompressible and compressible solvers, respectively, and the liquid-vapor interface is modeled as a sharp boundary subject to energy-jump conditions derived from first principles, without accommodation or tuning coefficients. Conjugate heat transfer through the tank walls is accounted for by solving the heat-conduction equation in the solid domain rather than prescribing external heat-flux conditions. The framework is validated against laboratory-scale LN2 and large-scale LH2 experiments, reproducing the spatio-temporal evolution of pressure and temperature without adjustable parameters. In both settings, the simulations identify two distinct regimes in self-pressurization: an initial heating-driven phase that establishes a self-similar temperature profile in the vapor, followed by an evaporation-driven phase in which the pressure rise is governed by the saturation relation. The comparison between these largely different scales motivated a revised scaling for self-pressurization, based on ullage thermodynamics. Finally, the influence of buoyancy was examined by reducing the strength of the gravitational body force, which revealed that natural convection modifies the duration of the transient heating phase but has a limited impact on the long-term pressurization rate. This analysis also clarifies the mechanism controlling the development of thermal stratification in the liquid. Overall, the segregated approach provides a predictive, parameter-free tool for analyzing cryogenic storage and offers a physically grounded basis for scaling self-pressurization across fluids, geometries, and heat-flux conditions.

title: Influence of dosing parameters and droplet profile fitting methods on static contact angle determination in TiO₂ nanofluids
abstract: Measuring the static contact angle (CA) is essential for advancing heat transfer technologies and materials engineering. This work investigates how dosing parameters—specifically liquid dosing rate (2, 4, and 6 µL/s) and droplet volume (20 µL)—affect the repeatability of goniometric measurements for TiO₂-water based nanofluids (0.2%, 0.5%, and 1 wt%). Experiments were carried out with a Krüss DSA25 Expert analyzer, and the results were assessed using both Type A and Type B uncertainty analyses. Droplet generation was carefully controlled, and changes in droplet geometry were monitored over time. Data from the initial transient phase (first 10 s) were discarded, and all-time series were synchronized to a common reference point. The contact angle was evaluated using three fitting approaches: ellipse, circle, and Young–Laplace models. The study showed that both the dosing conditions and the chosen fitting model substantially influence the measured CA values. Depending on nanofluid concentration and dosing rate, discrepancies between geometric and Young–Laplace methods reached about 10–15°. Boxplot analysis indicated that geometric methods exhibit greater scatter, reflected by larger interquartile ranges than those of the Young–Laplace model. The coefficient of variation was roughly 2–5% for the Young–Laplace method and 8–12% for the geometric approaches, demonstrating poorer repeatability for the simplified models. Overall, the results highlight that both experimental setup and data analysis strategy are decisive for reliable contact angle measurements in nanofluids.

title: Parametric estimation of heat transfer coefficient: Incorporating boundary losses for enhanced accuracy
abstract: Thermal regulation of structural components is critical to modern applications, particularly those subjected to erratic operating conditions and environments. For instance, space probe solar panels and electric vehicle battery packaging avail vascular-based active cooling via fluid circulation to safeguard these critical onboard assemblies from thermal overload during charging/discharging. To conduct systematic heat transfer studies—involving modeling and/or experimentation—and develop suitable designs, it is essential to estimate the convective heat transfer coefficient (HTC). While the convective HTC, herein denoted by h_conv, is a useful parameter, it is neither a material property nor a fundamental thermodynamic quantity, and is thus challenging to accurately estimate. Precise measurement of h_conv from thermal experiments requires either achieving adiabatic conditions (a theoretical ideal often not realized in practice) or quantifying boundary loss (a random and nonlinear phenomenon). Additionally, thermal measurements, such as those obtained with infrared (IR) imaging, are prone to noise, further complicating the calculation. To overcome these challenges, we propose a new approach that combines experimental transient thermal measurements (together with noise filtering techniques) and a parametric estimation method based on a reduced order model (ROM). This approach allows one to determine both the convective HTC and boundary loss simultaneously and systematically. Moreover, incorporating boundary loss into the calculation of h_conv enhances the accuracy, which in turn leads to higher fidelity numerical models that can be used to better understand and design more efficient thermal regulation systems.

title: Modelling the role of surface roughness in pool boiling
abstract: Intermittent liquid wetting has been observed during pool film boiling on rough surfaces, but the mechanisms governing wetting initiation remain unclear. In this study, the influence of surface roughness on wetting behaviour is investigated using experimental cooling curves and two-dimensional (2D) numerical simulations. A one-dimensional (1D) transient heat conduction model is used to extract wetting characteristics from experimental data, providing the onset temperature of wetting and the evolution of wetted patch size, represented by an equivalent circular radius. The wetted patch radius decreases linearly with increasing surface temperature, with similar slopes independent of surface roughness, while the onset temperature increases with roughness. To interpret the experimentally observed onset behaviour, 2D simulations were performed, focusing on heat transfer near roughness tips. The results show that wetting initiation is governed by the balance between conductive heat transfer within the roughness element and heat extraction through the liquid–vapour interface, which determines the temperature reduction at the roughness tip. Roughness geometry affects this local thermal balance by changing the conductive resistance and heat replenishment between the substrate and the tip, thereby influencing the onset of wetting. Together, the results show that surface roughness primarily affects wetting initiation, whereas the subsequent evolution of wetted area follows a nearly linear dependence on surface temperature.

title: A coupled thermo–hydraulic model with phase change and local thermal nonequilibrium for simulating freeze–thaw dynamics in fractured porous media
abstract: Seasonal freeze–thaw cycles pose major challenges to underground infrastructures in cold regions, where rock fractures exert strong control over subsurface fluid flow, heat transfer, and ice formation. However, the role of fracture–matrix interactions during freezing and thawing remains poorly understood. In this study, we develop a coupled thermo–hydraulic (TH) model with phase change and local thermal non-equilibrium (LTNE), formulated within a finite element framework, to investigate these processes in fractured porous media. The model is based on the discrete fracture network approach, where fractures are represented as lower-dimensional entities embedded within a permeable porous matrix. It can capture ice–water phase change, LTNE heat exchange between fracture fluid and the surrounding rock matrix, as well as latent heat effects and phase-dependent permeability in both fracture and matrix domains. Model verification is conducted against four benchmark problems, addressing fracture–matrix heat exchange under LTNE conditions, ice–water phase change under freezing and melting, and lower-dimensional fracture representation implemented in the proposed TH modeling framework. The model is further applied to problems of increasing complexity, from a single fracture to intersecting fractures and ultimately to a fracture network, to systematically elucidate the roles of freeze–thaw processes in fracture-scale permeability evolution and network-scale flow reorganization. Our results reveal a self-reinforcing feedback mechanism in which freezing blocks secondary pathways, focusing flow into major channels, which in turn suppress further freezing and sustain preferential flow. These findings have important implications for many hydrological, geophysical, and geotechnical applications in cold regions.

title: Molecular insights into thermal conductivity alteration of graphene oxide-Nafion nanocomposite membranes
abstract: Effective thermal management in Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells (PEMFCs) is essential for improving durability, performance, and water balance. This study investigates molecular mechanisms governing thermal conductivity (TC) enhancement in graphene oxide (GO) reinforced Nafion membranes under hydration levels ranging from λ = 3–15 and GO loadings of 0.8 wt% and 1.6 wt%. Molecular dynamics simulations predict up to a 12% increase in TC at intermediate-to-high hydrations ( λ =6–15), mainly due to strengthened hydrogen-bond networks and percolated water clusters. Cluster analysis indicates a transition from fragmented to percolated water domains above λ > 6, forming continuous heat pathways. This is supported by the pair interactions, revealing that GO’s hydroxyl groups anchor hydrogen bonds, enhancing local water structuring and connectivity. Negligible changes in water and hydronium mobility with the presence of GO emphasize that thermal enhancement arises mainly from phonon-mediated transport in such systems. However, at very high hydration ( λ =15) and low GO content, water-mediated heat transfer dominates, yielding a TC comparable to that of pristine Nafion. Also, the vibrational density of states (VDOS) results imply improved phonon coherence that weakens at λ = 15 with low GO. Additionally, the probability density function (PDF) results at λ = 15 demonstrate the formation of denser water shells with parallel orientations around GO, which weakens its contribution to heat transfer. Thus, GO plays a dual role in optimizing Nafion’s thermal behavior, which depends on the hydration level. The improved properties of the GO-reinforced membrane can benefit the electrochemical reaction rates in PEMFCs by reducing the temperature gradient across the membrane-catalyst interface.

title: Improved weighted residual equations for modeling heat transfer enhancement in thin film flows
abstract: A thin film flowing down a vertical wall develops large solitary waves at its free surface due to the Kapitza instability, which enhances heat transport across the film. In this work, two families of robust reduced-order models, one- and two-variable models, are developed to predict temperature profiles and heat transfer in falling films at moderate to large Reynolds ( R e ) and Prandtl ( P r ) numbers, owing to their relevance to industrial processes such as waste heat recovery. First, a set of one-variable models is formulated in terms of the interface temperature using an innovative weighted-residual formulation that employs high-degree polynomials. In this approach, reduced-order equations are obtained via Galerkin projections onto polynomials that closely represent dominant eigenfunctions of a disturbed temperature profile in a flat film. Linear stability analysis demonstrates a closer agreement with exact eigensolutions compared to previously proposed reduced-order models for falling films. While the one-variable model accurately predicts the temperature profile in nonlinear waves at low to moderate R e and P r , they deviate at high values of P r and R e , leading to non-physical temperatures at the crest of the solitary wave. To resolve this, two-variable models incorporating both the interface temperature and its curvature are developed. These models effectively capture the results of the linear stability analysis and the temperature profile near solitary wave crests formed at higher R e and P r . Further, the two-variable models do not exhibit unphysical interface temperatures and heat transfer values for experimentally satisfactory values of large R e and P r , a shortcoming typically observed in other weighted residual temperature models. While the two-variable models enhance the accuracy of interface temperature in this range, the simpler one-variable model remains effective for predicting the wall temperature and the flux. Consequently, the proposed models provide a computationally efficient alternative to time-consuming direct numerical simulations or costly experimental trials for obtaining reliable heat transfer estimates.

title: Molecular dynamics study of droplet condensation and movement on a wedge-shaped continuous gradient composite surface
abstract: Insufficient condensation and inefficient droplet removal on functional surfaces limit the performance of water harvesting and thermal management systems. To address these challenges, this paper employs molecular dynamic (MD) simulations to investigate the condensation and self-driven transport of water molecules (WMs) on wedge-shaped composite copper surface with continuous wettability gradients (WGs). The results reveal that both condensation efficiency and droplet mobility are governed by the effects of WGs, surface hydrophilic degrees, and vertex angles. Expanding the hydrophilic region and increasing vertex angle significantly enhance condensation efficiency, while larger vertex angles produce narrower and flatter droplet morphology that facilitates self-driven motion. Notably, continuous WGs outperform conventional fixed contact angle (CA) designs inside the wedge, with the 150/120–0° gradient achieving the highest performance, improving condensed of WMs by 26.3% and drainage numbers by 64.5% at a vertex angle of 14°. These enhancements are attributed to reduced energy barrier and driving mechanism arising from Laplace pressure and surface energy gradient. Overall, this study provides valuable insights into controlling and understanding droplet dynamics on structured surfaces, contributing to the design of surfaces with optimized condensation and drainage properties.

title: Experimental study of local heat transfer with oil jet on rib-roughened surfaces
abstract: An experimental investigation was carried out to characterize the local convective heat transfer induced by high-Prandtl-number oil jets impinging on rib-roughened surfaces, with relevance to the cooling of high-power-density electric machines. A dedicated experimental setup combining infrared thermography and an inverse heat conduction method was developed to provide two-dimensional heat transfer maps with high spatial resolution. The target plates consisted of alternating straight ribs and cavities, with cavity depths of kc = 35–105 µm and cavity fractions Fc = 20%–50%, where Fc here denotes the obstacle density (larger Fc implies a higher density of obstacles). Injection conditions covered 525 < Re < 1770 and 148 < Pr < 328. For the smooth reference surface, the measured distributions exhibited the expected radial decay of the Nusselt number, validating the methodology. On rib-roughened surfaces, the impinging flow became highly anisotropic: while the parallel direction to the ribs showed little deviation from the smooth case, the perpendicular direction displayed a strong enhancement of convective heat transfer, reaching up to 36% higher average values under the most favorable conditions. This improvement intensified with both geometric and injection parameters, revealing their combined influence. These findings provide new insight into the coupling between fluid dynamics and textured-wall geometry in localized oil-jet cooling applications.

title: Estimation of spatially varying thermal contact conductance in metal foam heat sink joints using measured pressure distribution
abstract: Generative AI has intensified the demand for advanced thermal management in electronic systems such as data centers, GPUs and high-performance processors. Metal foam-based heat sinks, including composite fin and phase change material (PCM)-integrated designs offer superior thermal performance due to high surface area and enhanced heat dissipation. However, accurate quantification of thermal contact conductance (TCC) between the solid heat sink base and the metal foam remains a key challenge.This study quantifies TCC at interfaces between copper substrates and metal foams of copper (10 and 20 pores per inch, PPI) and aluminum (20 PPI) under contact pressures of 1.5, 2.0, and 2.5 MPa. Three modeling frameworks were developed: the conventional Cooper-Mikic Yovanovich (CMY) model with nominal pressure and two modified CMY models integrating measured spatially varying contact pressure distributions. The third model, incorporating a pressure-scaling factor (mul), exhibited the best agreement with experimental temperatures, limiting deviations (Texp - Tsim) to ±0.7K, whereas other models showed differences up to 18.5 K and 9.25 K. Inverse heat transfer analysis (approach 3) yielded effective thermal conductivities and mul with high precision. For Cu-20PPI, Cu-10PPI, and Al-20PPI foams, standard deviations in conductivity (k) were 2.86%, 5.10%, and 0.49%, and in pressure scaling parameter (mul), 2.6%, 5.92%, and 0.08%, respectively. The proposed modified CMY model, calibrated for each metal foam type, enables accurate and computationally efficient prediction of interfacial TCC in metal foam-based heat sinks.

title: Prediction and uncertainty quantification of saturated flow boiling heat transfer coefficients in mini/micro-channels using Gaussian Process Regression
abstract: Accurate prediction of the heat transfer coefficient in saturated flow boiling within mini/micro-channels is essential for designing high-heat-flux thermal systems. This study develops a Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) model using a consolidated database of 11,469 pre-dryout data points from 41 sources. The dataset spans diverse working fluids and operating conditions representative of practical mini/micro-channel applications. Feature selection was conducted using permutation feature importance (PFI) and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values, and hyperparameters were optimized by maximizing the log marginal likelihood with an L-BFGS optimizer and early stopping. Compact GPR models were constructed for various covariance kernels. Notably, the ARD Exponential kernel achieved the best balance between predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration, effectively capturing the regime-dependent non-smooth variations of boiling heat transfer. Across the consolidated database, the optimized GPR exhibited a test MAE of 8.45%, outperforming conventional empirical correlations. When validated on previously unseen data, the GPR model demonstrated strong generalization capability, yielding an MAE of 17.35% and surpassing the performance of the Kim and Mudawar correlation showing MAE = 24.18%. These results confirm that GPR provides an accurate, interpretable, and reliable predictive model for predicting saturated flow boiling heat transfer coefficients under diverse and previously untrained operating conditions.

title: Investigation effects of medium thermophysical properties on dynamic Leidenfrost for superheated surface
abstract: The physical and chemical properties of droplets play a critical role in the dynamic Leidenfrost phenomenon on superheated surfaces and therefore strongly influence heat transfer efficiency. To investigate this effect, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were employed to examine how key physicochemical properties of droplets, such as boiling point, viscosity, and surface tension, affect their heat transfer performance upon contact with a heated surface. The results indicate that a higher boiling point can enhance heat transfer efficiency; however, this improvement depends on the relationship between the surface temperature and the droplet boiling point. In particular, when the boiling point approaches the surface temperature, the enhancement in heat transfer becomes less significant. Furthermore, an increase in droplet viscosity substantially suppresses heat transfer efficiency and prolongs the time required for the droplet to reach its optimal spreading state, regardless of the surface temperature. In addition, increasing the surface tension coefficient weakens the heat transfer performance by reducing the contact time between the droplet and the surface and accelerating the impact process; however, this negative effect becomes less pronounced at higher surface temperatures. Overall, this study provides a theoretical basis for improving droplet heat transfer efficiency on high-temperature surfaces.

title: Spatio-temporal analysis of sprays by using Phase Doppler Anemometry data
abstract: Spray characterization commonly relies on statistical quantities assuming quasi-steady behavior, although stochastic and instability-driven mechanisms govern atomization. Despite widespread application of Phase Doppler Anemometry (PDA), the temporal characteristics of sprays and their implications for modeling are unexplored. Deviations from Poisson arrival statistics indicate droplet clustering, i.e., time-dependent behavior. The present study investigates the spatio-temporal characteristics of an airblast atomizer using PDA datasets, including droplet size, velocity, and arrival time. Interparticle arrival time distributions are evaluated against theoretical Poisson statistics using chi-squared testing and effect size analysis. Multimodality is observed in specific spray regions, indicating pronounced clustering and temporal intermittency. K -means clustering combined with gap statistics quantifies droplet clusters across 10,800 datasets covering various atomizing pressures, temperatures, liquids, and spatial positions. Approximately 30% of datasets exhibit clustering, affecting up to 40% of droplets. Cluster occurrence depends on atomizing pressure and spatial position, while no clear dependence on preheating temperature was observed within the investigated range of conditions. After removing secondary clusters, the spray approaches quasi-steady behavior, indicating that clustering dominates unsteadiness in the core region, while mixing governs peripheral fluctuations. Despite the identified clustering in arrival times, the distributions of droplet size and velocity remain statistically similar across clusters, indicating that clustering reflects temporal intermittency rather than dynamic sorting of droplet populations. This supports a kinematic packing interpretation consistent with intermittency imposed by the carrier flow. The results demonstrate that neglecting clustering may bias spray statistics and modeling, emphasizing the need to incorporate temporal structures into advanced spray models.

title: Thermal characteristics of developing flow in an annular pipe
abstract: The paper investigates the behaviour of turbulent flow through a domain exhibiting an abrupt transition in cross-sectional geometry from a circular to an annular pipe using Large Eddy Simulation (LES). Three Reynolds numbers, based on the hydraulic diameter of the annular section, were selected, namely 8 900, 16 200 and 40 500, with an inner-to-outer diameter ratio of D inner / D outer = 0.5 and a Prandtl number of 4.327 (liquid water). Equal heat fluxes were applied to both the inner and outer surfaces of the annular section, ensuring a flux ratio q * = q ″ inner / q ″ outer = 1 . The results reveal significant flow laminarisation along the outer wall at the entrance of the annular section, driven by strong flow acceleration from the vena contracta, followed by its deceleration. In the locally retarded flow region near the outer wall, laminar and turbulent fluxes are both relevant. Farther downstream, as the flow redevelops a fully turbulent regime, turbulent heat fluxes become the primary driver. By contrast, the separated flow region adjacent to the inner wall displays turbulent shear stresses nearly an order of magnitude higher than those in fully developed annular flows. Consequently, turbulent fluxes are most significant at the inner wall. The heat transfer results obtained in this work allow assessment of Nusselt number correlations in developing annular flow, showing that the Gnielinski (2015, Heat Transfer Engineering , 36 (9), pp. 787–789 ) and Taler and Taler (2017, E3S Web of Conferences , 13, p. 02008), when combined with the Hausen distance correction, yield a good level of accuracy at the inner wall (10–30% relative difference).

title: Three-dimensional frost structures on fluorine coated silver iodide (AgI) micropatterns
abstract: Frost growth on silver iodide (AgI) stripes micropatterned surfaces is determined not only by the initiation of nucleation, but also by its growth kinetics after nucleation. In this study, these effects are investigated by comparing frost growth on three surfaces: bare silicon, AgI stripes on silicon, and fluorinated AgI stripes with modified wettability. Two-dimensional (2D) observations combined with three-dimensional (3D) frost reconstruction by the replica method reveal distinct growth behaviors on the three surfaces. Bare Si undergoes condensation freezing, forming dense and vertically oriented frost columns. In contrast, uncoated AgI stripes promote quick ice nucleation and lateral growth, producing frost with approximately 25% less ice volume and a characteristic horizontal wedge-like structure. For the fluorine (F) coated surface, lateral propagation is suppressed and frost grows predominantly upward, resulting in an approximately 30% increase in frost accumulation and the formation of vertically oriented columnar structures connected to the substrate through slender frost roots. These results show that nucleation activity determines where frost initiates, whereas surface wettability regulates the direction of frost growth, clarifying the distinct roles of nucleation activity and surface wettability in controlling frost morphology.

title: Offset dense jets in co-and-counter flow: Experimental and numerical study
abstract: This study investigates the mixing behavior of turbulent offset dense jets discharged into co- and counter-flowing ambient currents under varying confinement ratios. A comprehensive experimental campaign using planar laser-induced fluorescence (PLIF) was conducted for two densimetric Froude numbers, supported by Reynolds-averaged numerical simulations. The experiments reveal that co-flow produces smoother centerline decay trends and more asymptotic behavior, whereas counter-flow often triggers low-frequency oscillations, enhanced lateral spreading, and delayed decay. Confinement plays a central role: at small confinement ratios, the counter-flow jet forms persistent recirculation zones, suppressing flapping motions and reducing dilution; at larger confinement ratios, counter-flow promotes stronger unsteadiness and faster decay at sufficiently high current Froude number. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) was employed to examine the large-scale dynamics and revealed that counter-flow scenarios exhibit pronounced low-frequency flapping behavior, whose strength and spatial extent depend strongly on confinement. Numerical predictions captured the general trajectory and recirculation patterns but consistently over-predicted dilution, especially at higher current Froude number values. The combined results provide new insight into offset jets released into non-stagnant coastal environments.

title: Study on the scale effects of supercritical hydrogen leakage for different vessel volumes and typical orifice sizes
abstract: Under the high-pressure, low-temperature conditions relevant to supercritical hydrogen storage, the transient depressurization of a vessel through a leak orifice is strongly influenced by real-gas thermophysical-property variations and the large pressure ratio driving choked discharge. However, quantitative source-term characterization and scale-dependent trends for such supercritical blowdown scenarios remain insufficiently documented. This study considers a representative circular orifice and develops a one-dimensional, time-dependent leakage source-term model by coupling mass conservation with an isentropic choked-flow formulation. Thermophysical properties of hydrogen are evaluated using the Peng-Robinson real-gas equation of state, enabling non-ideal effects to be incorporated in a computationally efficient manner for the pressure range of interest. One-dimensional simulations are performed for vessels of 30 L, 50 L, and 100 L with an initial state of 80 K and 35 MPa to predict the transient in-vessel pressure and mass histories, together with time-resolved discharge source terms (e.g., mass flow rate and stagnation-state variables at the orifice). A fitted leakage coefficient Cdd is introduced to correlate the relative leakage rate with the geometric scale parameter V/A within one characteristic time constant. The results indicate that the leakage behavior can be categorized according to the order of magnitude of V/A distinguishing large-orifice, small-orifice, and micropore regimes. Within the investigated range, Cdd remains nearly constant in the small-orifice regime, indicating a stable scaling relationship between leakage dynamics and the geometric parameter V/A. The proposed model further provides practical source-term metrics, such as leakage duration and half-pressure-drop time, which can be used as inputs for subsequent hydrogen jet dispersion analyses and safety assessment.

title: Multi-phase and multi-species decomposition model for hydrogen peroxide in catalytic chambers
abstract: A mathematical model of the flow through a catalytic chamber to be used in rocket engines is presented. The model is based on a Lagrangian approach and a homogeneous description of the phases. The equation for the decomposition process is expanded to consider the pressure influence on the chemical reaction and the influence of the mass transfer effects (diffusion, adsorption and desorption). For the vaporization and the temperature determination the enthalpy is used. The pressure drop is calculated through a relation between the resistance coefficient and Reynolds number. Polynomial approaches are applied for the thermodynamic and transport properties. The heat transfer between the flow and the chamber wall as well as the flow and the catalytic material is considered. Finally, a comparison between the experimental test data and the simulation results is provided. The steady state values of temperature and pressure match the experimental data. The temperature data are in a range of 8 K, while the pressure data are in the uncertainty of the pressure sensors ( ± 1 bar). The transient behavior of the model shows a good agreement with the experimental data.

title: Numerical study of fouling effects in asymmetric flow field-flow fractionation for nanoparticle separation
abstract: Asymmetric flow field-flow fractionation (AF4) finds wide applications in nanoparticle separation. However, the selection of operating parameters often relies on experimental trials, and membrane fouling during repeated operation can significantly affect separation performance. In this study, a multiphysics numerical framework was developed to simulate nanoparticle separation in AF4, capturing both the focusing and elution stages under prescribed operating conditions. A fouling model was introduced to relate particle accumulation on the membrane surface to spatial variations in membrane permeability, allowing the coupled evolution of flow redistribution and particle transport to be analyzed. The results show that membrane fouling induces a spatially nonuniform crossflow distribution, which shifts the focusing position and reduces separation resolution. Additional sensitivity analysis further shows that cake-layer-induced reduction of the effective channel height can also deteriorate elution resolution. These findings provide mechanistic insight into fouling-induced separation deterioration and offer guidance for improving parameter selection and the operational robustness of AF4 systems.
