title: Internal flow condensation of R515B and R1233zd(E) in smooth and structured round mini channels
abstract: Flow condensation is a cornerstone of refrigeration systems, heat pumps, and electronics cooling technologies, and its enhancement is critical for improving efficiency and reducing heat exchanger size. Numerous enhancement strategies have been proposed for flow condensation, including micro- and nanostructured surfaces which have been investigated for their potential to promote condensate film redistribution. In this study, the coupled effects of tube diameter, refrigerant properties, and surface structuring on flow condensation performance are systematically investigated. Experiments are conducted in tubes with internal diameters ranging from 1.5 mm to 4.7 mm using two low-GWP refrigerants, R515B and R1233zd(E), on etched aluminum and etched copper surfaces. A counter-flow tube-in-tube facility is employed, with particular attention to the experimental challenges associated with small diameter flow condensation measurements, including flow oscillations, streamwise saturation temperature gradients, and uncertainty control. The results show that heat transfer enhancement is achieved only within a narrow vapor quality range governed by the interaction between condensate film thickness and surface feature size. Averaged over the highest vapor qualities (0.7-1), enhancements of up to 45% are obtained on etched aluminum tubes with a diameter of 2.4 mm, while etched copper tubes exhibit enhancements up to 55% with a diameter of 3.1 mm. Film thickness and flow regime analyses indicate that surface structures become flooded at high vapor qualities (x > 0.8), suppressing capillary-driven film redistribution and eliminating enhancement occurring at lower vapor qualities. These findings establish critical thresholds for effective condensation enhancement in structured tubes.

title: Correlation-informed neural networks for predicting flow boiling heat transfer coefficient in mini/micro-channels
abstract: In this study, we develop a correlation-informed neural networks (CINNs) framework for predicting flow boiling heat transfer coefficients (HTC) in mini/micro-channels, addressing key limitations of purely data-driven artificial neural networks (ANNs) models and traditional empirical correlations. The proposed framework integrates consolidated experimental data with an established universal correlation through a physics-informed loss function, enabling the model to leverage both data-driven flexibility learning and physically grounded constraints. A comprehensive database of around 17,000 data points, along with four representative universal correlations, is used to train and evaluate the CINNs model. A physics-weighting parameter is introduced to modulate the balance between measured data and embedded physical knowledge. Model evaluations demonstrate that the CINNs framework achieves markedly improved prediction accuracy relative to standalone empirical correlations and exhibits enhanced robustness compared to the purely data-driven ANNs model, particularly when the training dataset is limited. Uncertainty quantification analyses further reveal the sensitivity of the CINNs performance to the underlying physics model and the amount of available training data. In addition, tests on unseen fluids show that the CINNs model provides substantially better extrapolation capability than the ANNs model, highlighting the benefits of incorporating physics-based structure into the learning process. Finally, the CINNs framework is leveraged to refine an existing correlation (Kim and Mudawar) by learning consistent parameter adjustments, yielding an ≈4% improvement in predictive accuracy. Taken together, these results demonstrate that the CINNs framework offers a powerful and data-efficient approach for modeling flow boiling heat transfer in compact channels, providing a significant advancement over conventional methods

title: Dimensionless step-response identification of adsorber thermal dynamics
abstract: Experimental identification of effective thermal parameters is a prerequisite for benchmarking and scaling adsorbers because their transient response is governed by simultaneous heat-transfer fluid convection, distributed temperature gradients, and contact- and geometry-dependent heat-transfer pathways that cannot be reliably predicted a priori. Focusing on heat-transfer-only provides a necessary, first step toward subsequent coupled heat-and-mass-transfer identification in full adsorbers. In this study, the dimensionless parameters that govern the thermal dynamics of the adsorbers are identified by imposing a temperature step to the heat-transfer-fluid inlet and regressing the outlet transient. The adsorber dynamics is expressed in a compact dimensionless form governed by two groups: the number of transfer units ( NTU ) of the adsorber and the solid-to-fluid thermal-capacity ratio ( C r ). Even with only two parameters, the regression is ill-conditioned: multiple combinations of values return the same dynamics. To resolve this non-uniqueness, the trajectory fit is augmented with an analytically derived maximum-slope consistency constraint, with explicit regime handling across the slope-switch point. Verification on synthetic datasets spanning both noise-free and noisy signals shows that the physics-informed formulation substantially reduces the uncertainty on the parameters identified. Demonstration on finite volume-generated conjugate step-responses for an annular finned-tube adsorber confirms physically consistent trends between dimensionless extracted parameters and dimensional design features, validating the use of this method for characterisation of thermal dynamics in adsorbers.

title: Coupled heat and mass transfer in internally cooled silica gel-coated aluminum foam heat exchangers for dehumidification
abstract: Solid desiccant dehumidifiers offer significant potential for improved humidity control in buildings due to their ability to independently regulate latent (humidity) and sensible (temperature) loads upon integration in evaporative cooling systems or compression-based hybrid air-conditioning systems. However, adsorption of water vapor by desiccants is an exothermic process; the resulting heat of adsorption increases both the desiccant bed temperature and the temperature of the air flowing over the bed, thereby limiting the performance of desiccant dehumidifiers. To address this challenge, desiccant-coated heat exchanger prototypes were developed by coating silica gel onto aluminum foam substrates integrated with chilled water circulation for continuous removal of the heat of adsorption during the adsorption process. Prototype heat exchangers with two different pore densities (10 and 20 pores per inch (PPI)) and two different desiccant loadings (~10.36% and ~17.80%) were fabricated to investigate the effects of pore density and desiccant loading on adsorption performance. Experiments were conducted by varying the inlet air face velocity, chilled water inlet temperature, and chilled water flow rate to investigate the coupled heat and mass transfer characteristics of the prototype heat exchangers over a wide range of operating conditions. The underlying transport mechanisms were analyzed using transient desiccant bed temperature, outlet air temperature, and outlet humidity profiles. The results demonstrate that internal cooling significantly enhances dehumidification performance compared to the uncooled condition. For an adsorption duration of 5 min, the improvements exceeded 98% in cumulative adsorbed mass and 97% in dehumidification capacity. Pressure drop measurements revealed a strong dependence on desiccant loading. Overall, the study confirms the feasibility of employing internally cooled aluminum foam substrates to further augment the dehumidification performance of solid desiccant dehumidifiers.

title: Flow boiling of HFE-7000 in a microchannel array — Relation between heat transfer dynamics and flow patterns
abstract: This paper presents an experimental study of heat transfer during flow boiling of HFE-7000 in a microchannel array consisting of 10 channels having hydraulic diameter of 1 mm. Experiments covered saturation temperature of 50 ° C , mass fluxes varying between 400 and 700 kg / m 2 s , average wall heat fluxes of 30, 35 and 40 kW / m 2 and inlet subcoolings of 10 and 15 K. The study focuses on local heat transfer coefficients ( HTC l o c ), vapor qualities ( x l o c ) and recording flow patterns along the array. The novelty of the study is simultaneous analysis of local heat transfer and flow patterns. This approach allowed investigating if the slope of HTC l o c ( x l o c ) function and flow patterns are interchangeable indicators of the dominant heat transfer mechanism, be it nucleate boiling or convective boiling. In two-phase region HTC l o c behaved consistently — it decreased with vapor quality, and at approximately constant x l o c it decreased with higher mass flux, wall heat flux and lower subcooling. However, two different flow pattern groups were observed in this region — bubbly/intermittent and churn/annular. This contradicts a direct link between the flow patterns and the slope of HTC l o c ( x l o c ) function. Thus, these parameters cannot be used interchangeably to identify mechanism dominating heat transfer. Comparison with selected heat transfer models showed that they mostly fail to capture changes in HTC l o c . Results of the work supplement the knowledge on small-scale flow boiling of HFE-7000, and point to the profound influence of wall temperature uniformity and pressure drop on heat transfer coefficient behavior.

title: Numerical study of the ignition dynamics of a base bleed unit during the interior ballistics phase
abstract: The aim of this article is to study numerically the ignition dynamics of a Base Bleed (BB) unit during the interior ballistics (IB) phase. A Forward Facing Step case is studied under the physical conditions of the first instants of IB, in order to characterize the convective fluxes at the solid propellant surface of the BB. Large-Eddy Simulations are carried out with the CEDRE CFD code. The recirculation zone obtained in the flow significantly increases convective fluxes at the inlet of the BB channel. The instabilities generated by the recirculation zone have frequencies in line with literature. An unsteady solid propellant ignition model is then presented to take account of BB ignition. A parametric study is carried out to characterize the effect of this model's parameters on ignition time and steady surface temperature. A second case is proposed to study BB ignition in more realistic conditions using a dynamic mesh technique and an unsteady solid propellant ignition model applied to the BB propellant surface. It can be shown that the propellant ignites quicker at the inlet of the BB channel due to higher convective fluxes, corresponding to the location of the recirculation zone. The BB's global ignition time and the mass of propellant burned during the IB phase are then calculated.

title: Study on transient flow and thermal evolution of supercritical CO2 cooling in scramjets with pseudo-boiling theory
abstract: During prolonged and wide range hypersonic flight, the scramjet faces severe thermal protection challenges and the electricity demand of the vehicle is surging as well. To address these issues, the novel cooling medium supercritical carbon dioxide (sCO2) is employed, with the closed Brayton cycle embedded onboard. Using the validated SST k-ω turbulence model, this study performs transient simulations to systematically investigate the vital transient behaviors encountered by sCO2 cooling under unilateral extreme heating of scramjet wall. The pseudo-boiling theory is utilized to intuitively elucidate the evolution process, and the buoyancy effect is innovatively integrated to comprehensively elaborate the underlying mechanisms. Results indicate that the wall conduction tends towards steady-state in about 10-20 s since the heating commences, except for the particular region (around x = 0.25 m) in the upstream, where HTD is exhibited afterwards, which is mainly caused by the continuously grown VL layer that exerts a significant thermal resistance. In addition to the evaporation momentum force that dominates the formation of the VL layer, the buoyant force also imposes a transport effect to redistribute the VL fluid within the rectangular channel, especially in the deteriorated region where the buoyancy effects are salient.

title: Unified analytical framework and regime map for capillary rise in cylindrical assemblies adjacent to a flat surface
abstract: A generalized mechanics-based framework is developed to characterize capillary-driven equilibrium and meniscus morphology in geometrically constrained cylindrical assemblies, including double-cylinder, multi-cylinder, and cylinder–surface configurations. The model development and results focus on an array of cylinders adjacent to a flat surface as the most complex morphology. The proposed formulation introduces a consistent dimensionless representation in terms of normalized pitch, gap, and radius. This representation enables systematic exploration of the admissible equilibrium solution space across configurations, particularly for an array of cylinders adjacent to a flat surface. Regime boundaries are identified as transitions between mechanically feasible equilibrium states, arising from geometric constraints on meniscus continuity and curvature. To facilitate practical implementation, a compact approximation is derived, providing an accurate and computationally efficient surrogate for the full implicit solution (R² = 0.99, RMSE = 0.14). The model is validated against independent datasets from the literature and new experimental measurements obtained from a custom-built testbed, demonstrating agreement within 5 mm across a wide range of geometric and wetting conditions. Analysis of limiting case recovers classical solutions for two cylinders in contact with a surface, confirming the internal consistency of the framework. The results reveal that capillary rise is governed by a nontrivial coupling between geometric confinement and interfacial curvature, leading to distinct equilibrium regimes not captured by existing simplified models. The developed framework establishes a unified theoretical basis for capillary phenomena in constrained geometries and provides a basis for analyzing a wide range of interfacial systems, including fibrous media, porous structures, and microstructured surfaces.

title: Thermodynamic origin of root-like architectures in topology-optimized porous electrodes
abstract: Recent studies have shown that topology optimization can generate high-performing porous architectures, often exhibiting graded, branched, or root-like morphologies. However, the physical origin of these recurring structures remains unclear. In this work, we develop a theoretical framework linking reaction–diffusion transport, topology optimization, and nonequilibrium thermodynamics to explain the emergence of root-like porous electrodes. Starting from a simplified first-order reaction–diffusion model with porosity-dependent effective properties, classical relationships for effectiveness factor and characteristic penetration depth are revisited and extended to graded media. Scaling arguments are then proposed for branch spacing, root thickness, and root length by balancing axial reactant delivery with lateral consumption in the surrounding reactive matrix. A thermodynamic interpretation is further introduced in which the penetration depth represents a crossover distance beyond which transport-related irreversibility becomes increasingly dominant. Density-based topology optimization is then employed to maximize overall reaction rate under finite porosity constraints. The optimized structures evolve from uniform to hierarchical root-like networks, showing substantially improved utilization compared with conventional uniform porous layers. The predicted geometric trends are consistent with the optimized morphologies. These results suggest that root-like porous architectures are not arbitrary numerical artifacts, but physically meaningful responses to coupled transport, reaction, and thermodynamic constraints. The present framework provides mechanistic design principles for reaction-diffusion-limited porous electrodes.

title: Active flow and flame control using plasma-induced swirl in a bluff-body burner
abstract: A proper control of the flame and flow structure is required to enhance energy efficiency and stability of the flame. In this paper a new bladeless fully electrical swirler using Dielectric Barrier Discharge (DBD) plasma actuators to promote the flame stability and energy saving on industrial burners was developed, overcoming drawbacks of traditional mechanical swirlers under different operational conditions. The design consists of four Surface DBD (SDBD) plasma actuators, with a radial mounted configuration on a bluff body burner to impart tangential swirl. Three-dimensional reacting and non-reacting flame simulations were performed to assess the performance of the plasma-based swirler in flow and flame modulation. Velocity contours, flow streamlines, tangential and radial velocity fields, the temperature distributions, spatial mixing deficiency (SMD) and swirl number analyses demonstrate that the plasma swirler has a remarkable effect on the increase of mixing rate to drive flame propagation toward the bluff body wall in terms of better stabilization. Noteworthily, the outward plasma swirler configuration gained most improvement for 3.42% decrease in SMD and 16.2% increase in heat release associated with better combustion efficiency. This is attributed to the inner vortex structures associated with outward configuration possessing maximum integrated swirl number by maximizing tangential momentum distribution and minimizing centerline axial momentum flux. This study confirms the potential of plasma swirlers as an adaptive, mechanically simple, and highly effective solution for active flow and combustion control.

title: Computational investigation of total-enthalpy based conjugate heat transfer in particle-laden flows using lattice Boltzmann method
abstract: This work presents a comprehensive computational investigation of asmoothed profile-lattice Boltzmann method for particle-laden conjugate heattransfer (CHT) using a volume-of-body (VoB)–based virtual fluid formula-tion. The method is enhanced with a two-relaxation-time (TRT) collisionoperator, and a detailed Chapman–Enskog expansion is derived to estab-lish the connection between the lattice dynamics and the macroscopic ther-mal energy equation. The resultant CHT model, implemented in the open-source waLBerla high-performance software framework, is rigorously vali-dated against a suite of three-dimensional benchmark problems across a rangeof Prandtl numbers, including sedimentation of a cold particle in a thermallystratified fluid, catalyst-particle heating in a vertical channel, and effectivethermal diffusivity in particle-laden Couette flow. These studies demonstrateexcellent agreement with established numerical and empirical results, whilealso highlighting the enhanced numerical stability of the TRT formulationcompared to its single-relaxation-time (SRT) counterpart, particularly forhigh specific-heat ratios. The scalability of the implementation is assessedthrough extensive weak and strong scaling analyses performed on up to 512compute nodes of both CPU (LUMI-C) and GPU (LUMI-G) partitions ofthe LUMI EuroHPC system. The results show that the model scales ef-ficiently on both architectures, with GPUs delivering significantly reducedtime-to-solution, while CPUs exhibit higher parallel efficiency due to theircomputation-dominated runtime. These findings demonstrate that our im-plementation approach enables large-scale, fully resolved CHT simulationsof particle-laden flows involving millions of particles, which is essential tostudy complex local phenomena occurring in several natural and industrialsettings.

title: The liquid utilisation bottleneck in interfacial thermal conductance at metal/water interfaces
abstract: The purpose of this article is to identify a microscopic metric that correlates with the interfacial thermal conductance (G) at solid/liquid interfaces. The vibrational density of states (VDOS) Overlap is widely expected to correlate positively with G, yet it fails to do so at numerous systems, and at gold/water interfaces, it actually decreases with increasing G. Here, we use non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations of gold/water, copper/water, and aluminium/water interfaces over a range of solid/liquid interaction strengths (ε_SL) to explain this contradiction. We show that the VDOS Overlap is a contingent metric: its trend with ε_SL depends on the relative positioning of the interfacial solid and liquid VDOS distributions, which is set by the metal's Debye frequency. By comparing the spectrally decomposed heat flux (SDHF) to the VDOS within each medium, we find that the degree to which the interfacial liquid utilises its available vibrational modes (η_IL) increases monotonically with G across the three metals while remaining invariant with ε_SL within each metal. The liquid's capacity to receive energy from the solid, not the spectral similarity between the two media, is the primary bottleneck to G across the three metal/water interfaces studied. We also discuss how this metric helps quantify the utilisation of in-plane modes to transmit energy at the interface.

title: Ultralow and tunable thermal conductivity of parylene C for thermal insulation in advanced packaging
abstract: Parylene C thin films have significant applications in advanced packaging of microelectronics. Their thermal properties are critical for thermal management of electronic devices. However, a unified understanding of the tunable structure and the corresponding thermal conductivity is still missing. This study investigated parylene C thin films of varying thickness and post-annealing temperatures grown via thermal chemical vapor deposition. The ultralow thermal conductivity of as-deposited parylene C measured by time domain thermoreflectance (TDTR) is 0.10 W/m-K. The thermal conductivity can be tuned by post-annealing. Significant increase in thermal conductivity is observed in the annealed samples (0.18 W/m-K) which induces melting and recrystallization. The results of XRD and polarized Raman spectroscopy show that the enhanced thermal conductivity is due to improved crystalline quality and the change in chain orientations. The measured thermal conductivities of the as-deposited and annealed films are much lower than the values predicted by the Cahill minimum thermal conductivity model, which can be explained by the diffuson-mediated minimum thermal conductivity model. Parylene C is found to possess the lowest thermal conductivity among dense low-k materials. Our work provides guidance for the structural design of ultra-low thermal conductivity polymers and corresponding thermal design of electronics.

title: Effect of flow orientation on the thermohydraulic performance of a tapered open-manifold microgap heat sink during flow boiling of HFO1336mzz(Z)
abstract: In this study, the influence of flow orientation relative to the gravitational field on convective boiling behavior of R1336mzz(Z) was investigated. The microstructured heated surface was composed of fifteen pairs of Dual-V asymmetric microchannels and was combined with a tapered open-manifold, forming a heat sink with divergent cross-section. Flow boiling experiments with R1336mzz(Z) were conducted at saturation temperature of 33 °C and inlet degree of subcooling of 10 °C with the test section at five distinct positions, corresponding to vertical upward flow, inclined upward flow, horizontal flow, inclined downward flow, and vertical downward flow. For each orientation of the test section, four inlet mass velocity setpoints were selected, ranging from 100 to 600 kg/m²s, and all tests were conducted for increasing heat flux until the estimated heat transfer coefficient presented a sudden decrease. Top-view images of the two-phase flow in the heat sink were captured using a high-speed camera, in order to relate the topological phase distribution to the heat transfer coefficient and pressure drop behavior. Even though the investigated heat sink classifies as a microchannel under most criteria, the present results indicate that the flow orientation can change the mechanisms associated with the heat sink geometry that are responsible for the phase segregation and dumping backflows, which promote significant heat transfer enhancement, are influenced by flow orientation. In general, these effects become more pronounced under conditions of reduced mass velocity and heat flux.

title: Estimation of internal and external heat loads by inverse conduction analysis of internally-cooled turbine vane
abstract: Quantifying the cooling performance of real hardware, internally-cooled gas turbine parts is challenging due to their characteristic dimensions and thermal properties and to the limited instrumentation access to their internal, cooled surfaces. Inverse heat conduction analysis methods are used in this context to estimate the heat loads generated by an internal cooling system from measurements of the resulting external surface temperature distribution of the cooled part. Existing works in the turbine cooling literature rely on bench-top testing facilities that do not reproduce a relevant external aero-thermal load, thus limiting the types of cooled components that may be tested with realistic internal flow behavior. The objective of this study is to extend traditional inverse conduction analysis and to demonstrate experimental and numerical methods to estimate the internal cooling performance of a real hardware-like nozzle-guide vane operating with engine-representative internal and external thermal loads. Thermal transient tests conducted with the test article installed in a linear cascade wind tunnel generate the external surface temperature responses necessary for the proposed iterative post-processing procedure to estimate both the internal and external heat loads. In particular, this work focuses on the description of the experimental test procedures developed and of the numerical post-processing approach. Internal and external heat load estimates are presented for a series of test conditions defined by combinations of different cooling system Reynold's numbers and the tunnel's mainstream turbulence intensity. The results demonstrate sufficient sensitivity and robustness of the methods to suggest the possibility of studying more complex and realistic test cases.

title: Identification of multi-physical fields in solar-driven methanol reforming hydrogen production reactor with a novel grid reconstruction method
abstract: Solar-driven methanol reforming hydrogen technology represents an important pathway to realize the clean hydrogen generation. To address the challenges of the grid generation of particle packed beds and precise identification of multi-physical fields within the reactor, the study proposes a novel grid reconstruction method that enables grid division for particle packed beds. Compared with homogeneous model and particle-resolved model, grid reconstruction model has obvious advantages in multi-physical fields identification and the number of particles that can be calculated. A three-dimensional multi-physical fields model incorporating heat and mass transfer, fluid flow, and thermochemical reactions is then developed to investigate the impact of catalyst particle shape and critical parameters on hydrogen production performance. The results indicate that the packed bed composed of cylindrical catalysts exhibits 3.46% to 18.37% higher energy conversion efficiency, and 5.57% to 22.25% greater hydrogen production rate per unit mass of catalyst compared to those constructed with spherical and Raschig ring catalysts. When the steam-to-carbon mole ratio decreases from 1.5 to 1.1 and the inlet volumetric flow rate increases from 36 mL/min to 44 mL/min, both the energy conversion efficiency and hydrogen production rate progressively rise, reaching maximum values of 57.53% and 21.97 mmol/(s·kg), respectively. This study provides both theoretical foundations and design principles for constructing high-efficiency solar driven methanol reforming hydrogen production systems.

title: Numerical modeling of nitrogen transport and loss during laser powder bed fusion of high nitrogen steels
abstract: High Nitrogen Steels represent a highly promising material class for Laser Powder Bed Fusion, but their processing is challenged by significant nitrogen loss due to a drop in solubility upon melting. To systematically investigate the underlying degassing kinetics and nitrogen transport mechanisms, this study establishes a high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics model utilizing the Volume of Fluid method. The continuous species conservation framework accounts for convection-dominant transport, integrating a temperature-dependent nitrogen solubility limit and an interfacial mass transfer sink term at the free melt pool surface. The numerical model is successfully calibrated and validated against single-track experiments on Fe-15Cr-0.3C-N steel substrates across varying surface energy densities, demonstrating good agreement with both experimental melt pool geometries and a spatial nitrogen concentration profile measured via Wavelength Dispersive X-ray Spectrometry. The results reveal that the final nitrogen distribution across the melt pool depth is fundamentally governed by intense keyhole degassing coupled with complex convective transport. Marangoni convection drives nitrogen depleted melt backwards, inducing steep surface concentration gradients, while recirculation vortices transport the degassed melt deeper into the substrate. Using a novel Nitrogen Retention Index, parametric analysis demonstrates that higher surface energy densities prolong active surface degassing, thereby intensifying nitrogen loss.

title: An experimental study on the time dependence of diffusive mass transfer of single oxygen bubbles
abstract: In the vast majority of gas–liquid engineering applications, the liquid phase contains a range of dissolved gaseous species. These dissolved process gases transfer from the liquid phase to the gaseous phase countercurrent to the typically desired mass transfer of gas to liquid. In process design, the resulting change in the composition of the gaseous phase is usually neglected, although a temporal change in the composition of the gaseous phase can directly influence the mass transfer performance over time. The current fundamental study quantifies the mass transfer performance of oxygen bubbles to liquid phases saturated with another gas. For this purpose, the oxygen mass transfer from a bubble to degassed, helium-, nitrogen-, argon- and carbon dioxide-saturated water is studied. Light Sheet Fluorescence Microscopy is used as imaging system for Planar Laser-induced Fluorescence measurements of dissolved oxygen concentration fields, delivering local instantaneous Sherwood numbers, diffusion coefficients and mass transfer coefficients. For the first time, the study showcases that the mass transfer performance from a gaseous dispersed to a liquid continuous phase is independent of time if mass transfer occurs in one direction only. If mass transfer occurs in both directions, the mass transfer performance of the dispersed phase is significantly lower and its time dependence higher to liquids containing gaseous species with high solubilities, such as carbon dioxide in water. Furthermore, the results suggest that applying intrinsic values, such as diffusion or mass transfer coefficients, obtained for binary systems in multicomponent systems can lead to high uncertainty.

title: Experimental characterization of an additively manufactured supercritical carbon dioxide recuperator
abstract: The design, fabrication, and experimental characterization of a high-temperature, high-pressure recuperator heat exchanger for a supercritical carbon dioxide cycle are presented. The heat exchanger core consists of a pin array of different designs on the hot and cold sides. The headers are integrated with the core and feature an interwoven architecture that enables pure counterflow heat exchange in the core. A recuperator with eight pairs of hot and cold passages is fabricated using the laser powder bed fusion method with Haynes 282, a nickel superalloy. X-ray CT scan images were used to confirm that the internal passages were clear of powder and to characterize deviations of printed features from the design. Experiments were performed in a recuperator configuration with the hot side at a nominal pressure of 80 bar and an inlet temperature of up to 800 o C, and the cold side at a nominal pressure of 250 bar and an inlet temperature of 300 o C. Results indicate an effectiveness of 72.3% and a thermal rating of 44.08 kW, with a gravimetric density of 11.7 kW/kg. The experimental results were compared against a one-dimensional steady-state model of the recuperator. When actual measured dimensions of the pin array are used in the model, the mean absolute percent deviation between model and experiments is 2.25% for effectiveness and 2.32% for power. The hot and cold side pressure drop between model and experiments are within 11.2% and 11.6%, respectively. A genetic algorithm-based optimization using the validated model indicates that a total gravimetric density (heat exchanger core + header) of 35.6 kW/kg can be achieved at 80% effectiveness for a 267 kW heat exchanger.

title: Secondary flow and peripheral heat flux distribution in square channels with macroscopic random roughness
abstract: We perform numerical simulations of conjugate heat transfer in square ducts for two representative rough surfaces (grit-blasted and graphite) and two fluid–solid conductivity ratios, using both DNS and RANS with the Spalart–Allmaras model. The effect of the QCR extension is also assessed, with a smooth-wall case serving as a baseline. DNS captures the altered heat-transfer distribution and secondary flows caused by roughness, whereas RANS tends to circularize velocity and temperature fields, yielding parabolic Nusselt profiles with limited sensitivity to geometric details. The QCR correction improves RANS predictions for grit-blasted roughness, where secondary flows resemble the smooth case, but degrades accuracy for the graphite surface, where eddy orientation is reversed. Despite local discrepancies, RANS agrees well with DNS in global metrics, with errors typically below 5%. For the first time, the heat-flux distribution along the duct perimeter is examined in detail, revealing that it depends not only on the roughness intensity but also on its morphological characteristics. These findings support the use of RANS for average heat-transfer prediction in rough-wall CHT, while underscoring the need for high-fidelity simulations to resolve the spatial complexity introduced by roughness.

title: Investigations of the windage in an aero-engine drive cone cavity
abstract: This study experimentally and numerically investigates the windage in an aero-engine compressor drive cone cavity. It designs and constructs an adiabatic drive cone cavity experimental system with the capability to measure windage heating. The windage power of the drive cone cavity is obtained by calculating the overall airflow enthalpy rise. The experimental windage moment coefficient Cm results are compared to the predicted results of the drive cone cavity Cm models transformed from the classical rotating disk cavity Cm models. The computational fluid dynamics (CFD) method, validated by experimental data, is utilized to analyze the windage formation mechanism in the drive cone cavity. Based on the Cm modeling theory of classical rotating disk cavities and the CFD results of the drive cone cavity, a simplified drive cone cavity Cm model that better reflects the flow structure is developed. The research results indicate that the variations in windage heating and Cm with nondimensional mass flow rate Cw and rotational Reynolds number Reω exhibit opposite trends. The windage heating in the high-radius regions of the drive cone cavity is greater than that in the low-radius regions under the combined effects of viscous dissipation and main vortex entrainment. Simplifying the drive cone cavity Cm model based on the flow structure reduces the maximum absolute relative error of Cm prediction results from 29.1 % to 15.0 % and the average absolute relative error from 13.3 % to 8.2 %.

title: Influence of buoyancy and wall heat transfer in CFD modelling of liquefied hydrogen storage tanks
abstract: To employ liquefied hydrogen (LH 2 ) for large-scale storage and transportation of low-carbon energy, boil-off prediction in cryogenic tanks is crucial. Boil-off is driven by heat ingress from the ambient, which also leads to pressurization and thermal stratification in the ullage. In this work, a sharp-interface model is implemented in OpenFOAM and used to predict pressurization, stratification and boil-off rates at three different fill levels of an LH 2 tank. A buoyancy source term is also implemented and added to existing RANS models. This source term is shown to completely suppress turbulence in the ullage. We have performed a series of simulations, predicting pressurization rates and thermal stratification. The results were compared to the K-Site experiments and for the first time, reasonable agreement was obtained across all fill levels. The boil-off rate showed qualitative agreement with the experimental estimates but was underpredicted in magnitude. The effects of heat-flux distribution, thermal contact resistance and variable wall thickness are also assessed, and their impact was found to be significant. This motivates the need for improved thermal boundary conditions, as well as possible coupling with resolved thermal models of the tank structure and insulation.

title: Cold energy recovery and reuse in artificial ground freezing for large-scale projects: Experiments and numerical modeling
abstract: Artificial ground freezing (AGF) is widely used for temporary support in subsurface construction. Current practice allows the frozen ground to thaw naturally once structural support is no longer required, leading to uncontrolled and inefficient dissipation of stored cold energy. Large-scale, multi-phase construction projects, where frozen-ground requirements shift across spatial locations over time, offer an opportunity to conserve energy by reusing residual cold energy across the site. This study proposes a cold-energy recovery and reuse framework for sequential AGF, in which cold energy from a decommissioned frozen zone is extracted and repurposed to pre-cool or freeze adjacent ground. The approach uses a heat transfer fluid loop to recover cold energy from frozen ground and transfer it to unfrozen ground. In this study, a laboratory-scale experimental setup is established, and a transient numerical model is developed, validated, and exploited to simulate cold-energy recovery and reuse under various operating and ground conditions. The results show that between 11– 15 MWh of energy can be recovered from frozen ground under representative field conditions, which can significantly reduce the energy utilized to cool adjacent unfrozen ground by up to 80%. Furthermore, the study reveals an imbalance between the energy recovered and utilized, arising from the predominance of sensible energy recovery in frozen ground and the combined sensible and latent energy storage in unfrozen ground.

title: Numerical investigation of the effective heat transfer coefficient for red clay hollow bricks
abstract: This study presents a numerical investigation of the effective heat transfer coefficient in red clay hollow bricks, accounting for the combined effects of heat diffusion in the solid clay and natural convection and thermal radiation within the air-filled cavities. Heat conduction through the solid material is modeled analytically, while the convective transport in the cavities is solved using the Fast Boundary-Domain Integral Method. To enhance computational efficiency, the H2 -approximation is employed to reduce the cost associated with the boundary-domain integral formulation. A parametric analysis is carried out for bricks with varying numbers of cavities and under different temperature boundary conditions, enabling a systematic evaluation of their influence on the overall thermal performance. The results provide new insights into the interplay between cavity geometry, boundary conditions, and effective heat transfer mechanisms, offering guidance for the design and optimization of energy-efficient building materials.

title: Micro-scale multiphysics modeling of lithium-iron phosphate electrode in lithium-ion battery
abstract: This study aims to elucidate the mechanisms underlying capacity degradation in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) electrodes under conditions such as high discharge rate and different temperatures. By constructing a three-dimensional, microscale electrochemical-mass coupling model, the multiphase polarization and energy dissipation characteristics within the electrode we quantitatively analyzed. The results indicate that, under high-rate conditions, the extremely low electronic conductivity of LFP leads to a spatially reversed distribution of the reaction front, and the massive solid-phase voltage drop forces the reaction to abnormally concentrate on the current collector side. At low temperatures, the electrode suffers from multiple polarization penalties, resulting in a thermal dissipation discontinuity spanning several orders of magnitude. Although the reduced size of active particles significantly increases discharge capacity and smooths the current distribution at the macroscopic level, it leads to more extreme local agglomeration and exacerbates spatial heterogeneity. Due to limitations in the conductive network’s transport properties, a non-uniform gradient design of the conductive agent and binder (CBD) can lead to localized polarization degradation. This study reveals intrinsic mass transfer bottlenecks under extreme operating conditions and provides insights for optimizing the microstructure of high-energy-density electrodes.

title: Heat transfer in high-frequency electric resistance welding: Scaling analysis of isotherm location under a moving AC-Joule heat source
abstract: This work presents an in-depth theoretical analysis of heat transfer in a semi-infinite solid subjected to a moving AC-Joule heat source, with specific application to High-Frequency Electric Resistance Welding (HFW). The HFW process relies on intense volumetric heating from an alternating current (AC) source that decays exponentially with depth from the weld interface. While HFW tubular products accounted for half of all global pipe and tube production tonnage in 2022, a critical challenge remains in process control: predicting the location where a target temperature, such as melting, is first attained along the edge. To address this, the closed-form solution for the 2-D temperature field is presented and then normalized to establish a new dimensionless framework. This framework is governed by two new intrinsic groups: the Scott number (So), which captures the ratio of thermal penetration depth to the depth of the exponentially decaying AC-Joule heating, and the Haga number (Hg), which captures the ratio of AC-Joule heat generation to thermal conduction. Together, these groups delineate two asymptotic regimes dominated by either volumetric heating or thermal conduction. Through asymptotic scaling analysis and blending, a unified closed-form expression is derived to predict an isotherm's incipient location across all regimes without relying on empirical fitting parameters. A practical case study demonstrates how this model enables rapid, physics-based predictions of melting onset using standard process inputs such as current, material properties, substrate thickness, and mill geometry. This approach offers a computationally efficient, theoretically rigorous alternative to empirical trial-and-error or complex simulations for HFW process design.

title: A wavelet-neural network method for efficient and high-accuracy prediction of thermal responses in random composite materials
abstract: Efficiently predicting the thermal responses of composite materials with complicatedly random and highly heterogeneous micro-structures remains a significantly challenging issue due to the formidable computational cost by traditional numerical methods. This work proposes a novel wavelet-neural network method, which achieves highly efficient and accurate prediction of the temperature field in random composite materials. At first, high-fidelity databases with high-dimensional and highly complex mappings are established by multi-scale computer modeling and finite element simulation of random composite materials across a wide range of randomly microscopic configurations and material properties. Moreover, a key contribution of this study lies in introducing wavelet transform technique to preprocess raw large-scale databases while achieving data dimensionality reduction, data feature extraction and noise filtering. Furthermore, the optimized deep neural networks are further employed to establish the predictive models from dimension-reduced data, which are equipped with three advanced techniques: Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) Block, Spatial Attention Module (SAM) and Residual Connection enabling superior predictive performance compared to conventional neural networks. Finally, the computational efficiency and accuracy of the proposed wavelet-neural network approach are validated via extensive numerical experiments. Numerical results clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Specifically, it achieves a computational speedup ranging from approximately 19 to 260 times compared to finite element solvers. In detail, the method accelerates 2D cases by up to two orders of magnitude while maintaining a substantial 20 to 40 times acceleration for complex 3D scenarios. Furthermore, the model exhibits exceptional regression accuracy with an average coefficient of determination ($R^2$) exceeding 0.999 across all tested cases, while keeping prediction errors below 5% in multi-scale temperature responses. Additionally, when handling material property parameters with 3% Gaussian variations, this wavelet-neural network approach simultaneously exhibit strong capability in noise resistance. It can be summarized that this scalable and robust wavelet-neural network framework offers an efficient and high-accuracy tool for data-driven thermal prediction of random composite materials in real-world applications, and can be extended to predict other material responses.

title: Direct numerical simulation study of the effect of horizontal flow on mixed convection in porous media
abstract: A direct numerical simulation (DNS) study is performed on mixed convection in a chamber filled with a porous medium composed of staggered circular elements. Natural convection is driven by a temperature difference between the two walls, while forced convection is caused by a prescribed horizontal force. The Rayleigh number in the range 1000 ≤ R a ≤ 20000 , pore-scale Rayleigh number in the range 1.2 ≤ R a K ≤ 39.2 , Peclet–Rayleigh number ratio in the range 0 ≤ P e K / R a K ≤ 1 , Prandtl number P r = 250 , and porosity ϕ = 0.46 and 0.56 are considered in the DNS study. The DNS results reveal that pore-scale dispersion caused by natural convection is significant due to the large R a K . It enhances the merging of small plumes in the boundary layer and reduces the mega-plume number. The horizontal flow has two competing effects on heat transfer. It weakens vertical macroscopic advection and pore-scale dispersion, and thus reduces the heat transfer. However, it also weakens small-scale horizontal motions in the boundary layer, which prevents the mega-plumes from merging and enhances the heat transfer. Consequently, the mega-plume number increases at R a = 1000 as P e K / R a K rises from 0 to 1. At R a = 20000 , the mega-plume number increases as P e K / R a K increases from 0 to 0.1; however, it decreases as P e K / R a K increases to 1, due to strong dispersion caused by the horizontal flow. The overall effect of the horizontal flow is mainly to reduce the Nusselt number. The Nusselt number follows the scaling law N u ∼ R a a , where a can be approximated as a = 0.5 − 2.5 × 1 0 − 6 P e for the present DNS cases.

title: Parametric liquid-cooling design for Li-ion batteries based on flow regime analysis
abstract: This study presents a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) model to predict transient temperature distributions in a prismatic lithium‑ion polymer (LiPo) battery cooled by forced water circulation through four distinct cooling circuits during constant‑current discharge. A novel methodology emphasizes the influence of dimensionless parameters on thermal and electrical responses, addressing a gap in existing literature and improving understanding of battery cooling strategies. The cooling circuit is modeled as a recirculating system, reflecting practical implementations rather than the common open‑loop assumption, and capturing the additional instability and complexity inherent to recirculation. Transient electrochemical–thermal behavior is simulated using Newman’s pseudo‑2D approach, treating porous electrodes as a collection of equal‑sized, isotropic, homogeneous spherical particles. The model couples electrochemical dynamics with conjugate heat transfer in the cell and cooling circuit. Validation was performed in a controlled chamber using experimental measurements and infrared thermography during discharge; simulated temperature, state of charge, and voltage curves were compared against experimental data. Results show strong agreement between simulations and experiments, demonstrating the model’s reliability for predicting LiPo battery behavior and their cooling circuits. Key battery parameters — effective capacity, specific energy density, specific heat capacity, electrical conductivity, and specific thermal capacity — were carefully estimated and validated to provide reliable reference values for modeling batteries of the same type. By systematically analyzing the role of relevant parameters —temperature, Reynolds number, flow velocity, heat flux, and pressure— on battery–cooling interactions, the model analyses their relative effects and provides actionable guidance for optimizing thermal management strategies in battery applications. This research provides practical value for battery designers and engineers developing systems that integrate batteries, facilitating improved efficiency, performance and safety.

title: Prescribed wall-heat-flux control of blockage and impulse in a rarefied micro-nozzle
abstract: Prescribed wall heat flux provides an active route for controlling rarefied micro-nozzle flows, but its effect is governed by the coupled wall--bulk thermal response rather than by the imposed flux alone. This work uses direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) simulations to study nitrogen flow in a converging--diverging micro-nozzle with cooling, adiabatic, and heating applied on the diverging wall. The imposed heat flux is scaled by the inlet kinetic-energy flux, $E=0.5ρ_i U_i^3$, giving $Q_w/E$ from $-10.5\%$ to $97.3\%$; this range spans moderate cooling, weak-to-intermediate heating, and a near-unity thermal-forcing regime. Wall and mass-flux-weighted bulk temperature profiles, film-temperature-based Nusselt and local-viscosity Brinkman-type diagnostics, gradient-length Knudsen indicators, mass-flux thickness, thrust decomposition, and proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) of signed numerical schlieren are analyzed. The results show that heating creates strong wall--bulk stratification: the wall temperature exceeds five times the inlet value, while the bulk temperature responds more gradually. Cooling cases contain locations where $T_w-T_b$ changes sign, making the local Nusselt-type response singular; the raw singular behavior is retained for diagnosis and a validity mask is used only for comparative plotting. Heating contracts the effective mass-carrying core, increasing aerodynamic blockage and reducing mass flow rate. However, strong heating increases the specific impulse from $156$ s to $201$ s because thermal and pressure-thrust augmentation outweigh the mass-flow penalty. The internal compression feature evolves into a finite viscous--thermal compression zone, and its heat-flux-parametric response remains low-dimensional, with the first two POD modes capturing more than $97\%$ of the fluctuation energy.

title: A Kalman-based identification framework for estimating thermophysical properties in transient layered heat conduction systems
abstract: Estimating thermophysical properties from indirect observations is a classical inverse problem in transient heat conduction, especially in layered systems where heat diffusion depends on material properties, interfaces and boundary conditions. This study develops a Kalman-based framework to estimate thermal conductivity and volumetric heat capacity from surface temperature time series. The method couples a one-dimensional transient heat conduction model with a batch assimilation strategy, in which the surface temperature time series is assimilated in a single EKF update at each identification iteration. The estimator operates on a parameter-only state, while temperature fields are generated by the forward model. The nonlinear parameter-to-temperature mapping is linearised using surface temperature derivatives, and the EKF covariance provides conditional uncertainty indicators. The framework is first assessed on a synthetic single-layer conduction problem designed to analyse identifiability under controlled excitation. Both thermal conductivity and volumetric heat capacity are recovered within 2 % of the reference values, with conditional EKF uncertainty interval half-widths below 3 %. Sensitivity analyses show that heat capacity identification requires sufficient temporal resolution to capture transient attenuation and phase shift. The method is then applied to a multilayer wall-like benchmark. The total thermal resistance is identified with an error of about 4 % over 24 h, and its uncertainty interval contains the reference value. Local identifiability indicators show that total resistance and dominant conductive behaviour are well constrained, whereas several layerwise properties remain correlated. These results support batch EKF assimilation as a computationally efficient framework for thermophysical property identification with covariance-based uncertainty and identifiability indicators.

title: Machine learning-based prediction of condensation heat transfer of low-GWP refrigerant R455A in an industrial plate heat exchanger
abstract: Accurate prediction of condensation heat transfer for low-global-warming-potential refrigerants remains challenging because experimental data are limited and conventional correlations often struggle with zeotropic mixtures such as R455A. This study develops machine-learning models to predict the average condensation heat transfer coefficient of R455A in an industrial chevron-type plate heat exchanger using experimentally obtained data. To address data scarcity while avoiding information leakage, an experimentally bounded synthetic data augmentation approach was applied within a 5-fold cross-validation framework. In each validation cycle, synthetic data were generated only from the corresponding real training portion, while the real validation portion was kept unseen during synthetic-data generation, scaling, model training, and parameter tuning. Several regression models were compared under REAL-only, SYN-only, and COMBINED training scenarios using 5-fold out-of-fold real experimental predictions. The REAL-only SVR (RBF) model produced the lowest numerical cross-validation error, while the COMBINED SVR (RBF) model was retained as the representative augmented-data model because it directly evaluates the proposed real-plus-synthetic learning framework. In the COMBINED scenario, SVR (RBF) achieved an R 2 of 0.9589, RMSE of 0.0482 kW m −2 K −1 , and MAPE of 4.38%. The representative COMBINED model was also benchmarked against Shah, Dobson–Chato-style, and Cavallini-style reference correlations on the same real experimental samples, showing lower prediction error than the conventional/reference methods. SHAP analysis was used as a model-interpretation and verification tool to confirm that the predictions were mainly governed by heat flux, vapor quality, mass-flux/Reynolds-related variables, and temperature-dependent properties. The results demonstrate that the proposed data-driven framework can provide accurate R455A condensation heat-transfer prediction within the tested plate heat exchanger operating range.

title: Directional pulsation characteristics of buoyant diffusion flames in crossflow using three dimensional modal decomposition
abstract: In this study, we present results from a computational analysis of buoyant diffusion flames in crossflow at conditions relevant to wildland fires. We examine the scaling relationship between the crossflow Froude number ( Fr c ) and Strouhal number ( St ), where the latter is commonly used to characterize the frequency of flame pulsations. The analysis is based on three-dimensional (3D) large eddy simulations (LES) for five sets of conditions spanning three orders of magnitude in Fr c . The simulations were performed using a computational framework that includes adaptive mesh refinement, reactions, and conjugate heat transfer between gas and solid phases. The proper orthogonal decomposition method of snapshots is used on 3D horizontal and vertical velocity data to extract dominant coherent spatial and temporal structures in the four lowest Fr c cases, providing a method that is measurement location agnostic and capable of extracting directional information on pulsation characteristics. We find a St = 0.37 Fr c − 0.42 relationship using the results from the horizontal velocity data, and a similar scaling for the vertical velocity except for the lowest Fr c , which was the most vertically-oriented flame. In this case, we observe a decoupling of the dominant horizontal and vertical flame pulsation characteristics, likely due to a regime transition between a flame strongly interacting with a crossflow and a purely vertically oriented buoyant jet flame.

title: Visualizing the onset of dry-out and gap-induced intermittent boiling in horizontally oriented annular-screen wicked heat pipe: Comparative analysis with screen wick and thermosyphon
abstract: This study clarifies how wick architecture governs dry-out resistance and flow instability in horizontally oriented heat pipes, which is directly relevant to passive heat removal in heat-pipe-cooled reactor systems. The onset of dry-out and internal two-phase behavior were compared for an annular-screen wick heat pipe, a conventional screen-wick heat pipe, and a wickless thermosyphon under the same geometry and operating conditions using synchronized high-speed visualization, wall-temperature measurements, and condenser-side heat-removal analysis. The results show that the annular-screen wick provides the strongest resistance to dry-out because the annular gap acts as both an additional liquid reservoir and a low-resistance liquid return path. Under ethanol operation, the underfilled screen wick reached local dry-out at 100 W power input, whereas the annular wick sustained stable operation to higher heat input and maintained a much smaller pressure-drop requirement, remaining near 54 Pa even at the onset of dry-out, while the screen wick already reached about 195 Pa at 100 W. The wickless thermosyphon showed the strongest circumferential maldistribution, with an evaporator top-to-bottom temperature difference of 80.6 °C, compared with 48.6 °C for the annular wick and 51.6 °C for the screen wick. A distinct intermediate instability was observed only in the annular-wick cases, where vapor generated in the annular gap intermittently blocked the liquid return path, causing irregular temperature oscillations and repeated rewetting. Among the tested fluids, water provided the largest capillary margin and the best thermal performance; the annular-water case showed a capillary margin of about 1501.7 Pa, while the maximum effective thermal conductivity reached about 1075 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ for screen wick, compared with about 131.1 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ for the wickless case. These findings show that annular-screen wicks substantially improve dry-out tolerance in horizontal heat pipes, although their design must also account for annular-gap-induced intermittent boiling instability.

title: Comprehensive analysis of scalable anti-frosting and anti-corrosion heat exchanger coatings
abstract: Frosting and corrosion are two key degradation mechanisms limiting the performance and durability of heat exchangers. Previous studies have typically investigated anti-frosting or anti-corrosion strategies separately under idealized laboratory conditions, with limited consideration of their combined performance in practical operating environments. Here, we systematically investigate twelve flat aluminum-based surfaces spanning hydrophilic (HPL) to superhydrophobic (SHPB) wettabilities by separately evaluating their anti-frosting and anti-corrosion performance and comprehensively comparing their overall performance. Among the superhydrophobic coatings, the best-performing surface (SHPB-1), fabricated by HCl etching, hydrothermal treatment, and heptadecafluorotetrahydrodecyltrimethoxysilane coating, prolonged the anti-frosting duration by approximately 3470% relative to the bare surface and by 460–1350% relative to conventional hydrophobic coatings under ambient conditions. Under forced-convection, low-temperature conditions, the corresponding improvements reached at least 600% and 140–820%, respectively. Microscale analysis shows this surface exhibits fewer but longer inter-droplet ice bridges and greater cumulative bridge length. Combined with the effect of ice bridge suspension, the ice bridging speed is reduced to approximately one-eighth of that on a hydrophilic surface. Despite the absence of a direct correlation between corrosion resistance and wettability, SHPB-1 exhibits a considerably low corrosion current density and the fifth-lowest mass loss among all tested coatings across two corrosion evaluation methods. Cost analysis further shows that SHPB-1 possesses the lowest material cost (∼2.9 $/kg) among the hydrophobic and superhydrophobic coating candidates. By comprehensively considering anti-frosting performance, corrosion resistance, fabrication cost, and processing complexity, SHPB-1 provides a well-balanced combination of anti-frosting capability and corrosion resistance, making it a promising coating for practical heat-exchanger applications. Rather than identifying a universally optimal coating, this study establishes a practical framework for balancing anti-frosting performance, corrosion durability, and fabrication cost in the design of heat exchanger coatings.

title: Wide-field quantitative mapping of thermal properties and structural defects at deeply buried interfaces
abstract: Thermal interface materials (TIMs) are crucial for thermal management in advanced electronic packaging, while buried voids or nonuniform bonding at interfaces can significantly deteriorate their heat dissipation performance. Pump-probe thermoreflectance techniques provide non-contact and high-resolution thermal probing, but conventional implementations are limited by shallow thermal penetration depth (TPD), making it difficult to access and quantitatively resolve thermal transport at deeply buried interfaces. Herein, we developed a high-throughput thermoreflectance strategy for rapid, quantitative interfacial thermal mapping of deeply-buried TIMs, by leveraging on adaptive heating spot size and modulation frequency, coupled with TPD, and integrating automated large-area scanning with unsupervised K-means classification. We apply to two representative TIM systems, namely thermal gel and indium foil, both deeply-buried under silicon slides with tens of micrometer thickness. The two-dimensional mappings exhibited thermal resistance distributions with high spatial resolution, where local structural defects can be identified clearly. Cross-validation is performed with acoustic microscope and X-ray imaging, confirming its capability for TIMs defects characterization. Moreover, heat-diffusion-amplified contrast even enables finer defects detecting that are otherwise undetectable by acoustic or X-ray imaging. Compared with traditional thermoreflectance implementations, this approach enables quantitative thermal transport properties resolving and interfacial defects detecting at deeply-buried interfaces, and is particularly efficient for structural quality evaluation of large-volume advanced packaging.

title: Physics-informed neural networks for planar interface evaporation: Forward, inverse, and parameterized modeling
abstract: In this work, we develop physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to model two-phase evaporation of a planar liquid-vapor interface by solving the unsteady one-dimensional Stefan problem in forward, inverse, and parameterized settings. The governing physics formulation couples the vapor volume-of-fluid (VOF) transport equation with the mixture energy equation through heat and mass transfer source terms. To enable stable coupling with a diffuse-interface and an energy-jump-based phase change model, we introduce a modified energy-intensity transfer source term. For the forward problem, the deep neural networks are trained solely from the governing physics and the prescribed initial and boundary conditions, without requiring labeled solution data. The forward PINNs solver is systematically evaluated with respect to collocation-point resolution, the energy-intensity coefficient, and the critical vapor volume fraction threshold, and it demonstrates robust predictions with minimal sensitivity to these training and model parameters. In addition, the framework accurately captures sharp interface motion associated with strong interfacial temperature gradients. Forward predictions of interface evolution and temperature fields under varying boundary conditions and phase properties agree closely with analytical solutions across all cases. For the inverse problem, a data-driven term based on VOF profiles from theoretical solutions is incorporated into the total loss. The inverse PINNs framework is then used to infer unknown boundary conditions (wall superheat temperature) and thermophysical properties (vapor thermal conductivity and latent heat) during training. The inferred parameters are recovered with errors below 7%, even in the presence of measurement noise. Finally, we extend the approach to training across a multidimensional parametric space to produce full field temperature and phase VOF solutions, highlighting its potential over traditional two-phase modeling methods.

title: Evaluation of surface‑area requirements for air‑cooled remote condensers
abstract: Accurate condenser surface-area determination is a critical aspect of HVAC design. This is particularly challenging for air-cooled remote condensers operating with zeotropic refrigerants, where temperature glide and subcooling significantly influence the heat transfer. Existing methods offer limited transparency in engineering application or rely on oversimplified LMTD-based formulations, which represent these effects with insufficient physical rigour. This study addresses both shortcomings through a closed-form analytical framework using the LMTD method subphase-wise to dry air-cooled remote condensers. A geometry-independent temperature-potential utilisation factor (η cond ) is introduced, enabling explicit calculation of the required surface-area, the corrected logarithmic mean temperature difference, and the theoretical minimum surface. Notably, when the air-side capacity rate is the smaller of the two, η cond is identical to the heat-exchanger effectiveness ε, enabling a single-step ε–NTU analysis of the entire condenser. Sensitivity analysis in a case study reveals that the subcooling region exhibits a fundamentally distinct parameter hierarchy, with the subcooling temperature dominant rather than the general inlet air temperature. Combined variation of the four theoretically adjustable parameters achieves surface-area reduction of up to 47.4%, whereas the most accessible engineering combination results in a 35.7% reduction. These findings necessitate the accurate LMTD formulation, as conventional LMTD simplifications introduce systematic errors of 56–59% overprediction and 48–57% underprediction. Validation against manufacturer data and literature sources confirms deviations below 1%. The presented transparent analytical framework supports engineering decisions for dry air-cooled condensers, including pre-design assessment, manufacturer selection verification, and fan-control strategy development.

title: A generalized formulation of local convective heat transfer in single-phase forced convection: Definition and verification
abstract: Addressing the long-standing issue of inconsistent definitions for local heat transfer coefficients in external and internal flows in single-phase forced convection heat transfer research, this study, from a global perspective of energy transport, proposes a local spatial convective heat transfer coefficient (LSCHTC) based on a constant inlet temperature, establishing a generalized characterization method for local heat transfer characteristics in both internal and external flows. By introducing the energy flux vector and energy flow tube model, it is revealed that the LSCHTC can represent the comprehensive transport efficiency of energy flow tubes between the inlet and specified wall positions. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this parameter and its reciprocal, the local specific thermal resistance (LSTR), clearly reflect​ variations in energy transport resistance along the flow direction and accurately identify​ heat transfer bottlenecks. The distribution of LSCHTC is not affected by the specific values of uniform wall temperature and wall flux boundary conditions but depends solely on flow and geometric conditions. And this distribution could directly and uniquely determine the wall heat flux or temperature distribution, providing a clear basis for optimizing heat transfer design. Additionally, through case studies on surface modification for external flow and channel geometry optimization for internal flow, it is verified that actively designing and optimizing the distribution of LSCHTC can effectively enhance local heat transfer intensity or improve wall temperature uniformity. Therefore, the proposed generalized local convective heat transfer coefficient, defined with a consistent benchmark and clear physical significance, is expected to provide​ an effective tool for performance evaluation, bottleneck diagnosis, and optimization design in single-phase forced convection.

title: Advances in the analysis of transient heat transfer experiments using multiple thermochromic liquid crystals
abstract: Transient heat transfer experiments that employ thermochromic liquid crystals (TLCs) provide high‐resolution surface‐temperature data but are hampered by noisy intensity signals, non‐ideal fluid‐temperature steps, and the challenge of resolving multiple TLC responses at pixel level. In this paper we introduce a fully automated analysis framework that (i) smooths and baseline‐corrects raw video data with a Whittaker‐algorithm whose regularisation parameter is explicitly linked to the signal density, (ii) identifies multiple intensity peaks per pixel via interval‐wise detection, and (iii) evaluates the local convective heat transfer coefficient using a stepwise‐partial‐integration (SPI) formulation of Duhamel’s principle. For each pixel, the heat transfer coefficient is determined for each individual TLC indication; the final value is formed by an inverse‐variance weighted average, guaranteeing that the most reliable indication dominates.The methodology is applied to a rotating two-pass cooling channel coated with a stack of two different narrow‐band TLC layers. Compared to conventional analysis using semi-infinite walls, the proposed workflow significantly improves the standard method by automatically detecting the peaks of multiple narrow-band TLCs. To illustrate the benefits of multiple TLCs, the additional information is used in this work to reduce the measurement uncertainty of the experiments. This is feasible because the selection of the optimal indication temperature for the TLCs depends on the heat transfer coefficient and the driving temperature difference at each individual point. Consequently, the results are evaluated post-experiment and weighted according to their respective standard deviations. This entire workflow enables multi-parameter analyses to be carried out in order to determine further variables from single experiments.

title: Scalable prediction of synthetic jet impingement cooling via a modular reduced-order machine learning framework
abstract: Synthetic jet (SJ) impingement cooling is a promising technique for enhancing convective heat transfer in compact thermal management systems. While the behaviour of single jets is well understood, practical applications require multiple jets operating in close proximity. In such configurations, strong nonlinear interactions between neighbouring jets significantly alter the flow structure and cooling performance, making accurate prediction challenging. This study develops an integrated computational, experimental, and machine-learning framework to predict the thermal behaviour of multi-SJ arrays. Transient CFD simulations, validated using hot-wire anemometry, are employed to characterise jet dynamics and generate a dataset spanning key non-dimensional parameters, including Reynolds number ( R e ), the jet-to-surface spacing ( 𝐻 ⁡ / 𝐷 ), lateral spacing ( 𝑆 / 𝐷 ), stroke length ratio ( 𝐿 / 𝐷 ), and actuation frequency. Conventional data-driven models trained on single-jet data fail to generalise to multi-jet configurations, while models trained on combined datasets remain restricted to fixed geometries. To overcome this limitation, a Modular Jet-wise Reconstruction framework is proposed, in which local single-jet predictions are superposed and augmented with an interaction-aware correction model to capture nonlinear jet-jet effects. The proposed framework enables accurate prediction across the investigated range of varying inline jet configurations without retraining, while achieving a computational speed-up of approximately 1 0 7 compared to transient CFD. This provides a computationally efficient framework for multi-jet cooling within the investigated configuration and parameter ranges and enables rapid design exploration.

title: Scalable surface structuring of stainless steel plate heat exchangers using chloride-based chemical etching for enhanced two-phase heat transfer
abstract: Heat exchangers play a key role in the functioning of industry. Improving the thermal-hydraulic effectiveness of heat exchangers is essential for optimizing energy efficiency. This study develops a passive method to enhance stainless steel heat exchanger performance using a highly scalable surface modification technique through static chemical etching with a chloride-rich custom-formulated etchant solution. The etching process chemically modifies the surface via Cl− and H+-induced passive film breakdown, Fe3+-driven oxidation, and Cu removal, leading to exposed metallic Fe and Cr and the formation of micro/nanoscale surface structures. Thorough analysis of etching reaction mechanisms and the resultant microstructures are obtained by quantifying micro and nanostructured surface morphologies using scanning electron microscopy, and focused ion beam sectioning. Additionally, X-ray diffraction, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy were performed to evaluate the surface chemistry prior to and after etching. Evaporation tests were performed on unetched and etched Cu-brazed stainless steel 304 plate heat exchangers, having surface roughness values of 0.8 μm and 5.2 μm, respectively. Flow boiling experiments with R-134a refrigerant revealed that the etched heat exchangers achieved a 54% enhancement in flow boiling heat transfer coefficient compared to their unetched counterparts, particularly at low vapor qualities. The improvement is attributed to an increased density of nucleation sites on the etched surface, which facilitates more frequent and smaller bubble formation, thereby enhancing nucleate boiling. These findings highlight the effectiveness of chemical etching as a scalable, rapid, and low-cost surface modification method for advanced manufacturing of next generation heat exchangers.

title: Laser-processed wickless vapor chambers harness phase change to enable forced-air cooling of high-heat-flux electronics
abstract: Traditional electronics cooling approaches often employ fins placed directly on top of heat-generating elements (e.g. CPUs or GPUs). While such methodologies are often sufficient to handle general heat loads, they prove insufficient in scenarios that involve smaller hotspots generating considerably higher thermal heat fluxes, i.e., of the order of hundreds of W/cm2. We develop a thermal test-bench capable of generating extremely high heat fluxes from two switching MOSFETs – emulating real-life operational scenarios. Thereafter, we show that incorporation of optimized wick-free vapor chambers (VCs), comprising of wettability-patterned, laser-textured evaporators and condensers, can effectively act as enhanced phase-change heat spreaders, reducing overall heat fluxes at the heat ejection site, and therefore enabling the deployment of traditional cooling methodologies, like forced-air circulation. The optimized VCs had consistently low thermal resistances of 0.09 K/W even at die heat fluxes of 400 W/cm2. Interestingly, these devices show no variation of thermal resistance with change in heat input, with the lowest measured thermal resistance being 0.04 K/W at ~50 W/cm2. Further, numerical simulations attest to the improved performance of these devices on incorporation of wettability patterns. An iterative numerical algorithm coupled with a CFD solver determines the orthotropic conductivities of the wettability-patterned heat spreaders enabling their rapid characterization and testing before experimental development. The present methodology highlights the role and importance of wick-free VCs, along with their advantages over traditional wick-lined VCs in air cooling of high-heat-flux electronic components.
